articles.title: Fio do Professor Felipe Nunes: análise da pesquisa Quaest para presidente de 21 de setembro | G1
articles.standfirst: Diretor da Quaest e professor da Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV), Felipe Nunes avalia momento atual da corrida pelo Palácio do Planalto.
articles.summary: Diretor da Quaest e professor da Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV), Felipe Nunes avalia momento atual da corrida pelo Palácio do Planalto.
articles.body:
1. Em nova pesquisa Quaest ( clique aqui para ver os dados ), Lula e Flávio aparecem, pela primeira vez, tecnicamente empatados no limite da margem de erro (37% x 33%) em cenário de 1º turno. Cury continua oscilando para baixo (6%). Os outros candidatos somam 9%. Indecisos são 8%; e 7% dizem que não vão votar em ninguém.

Fio do professor Felipe Nunes - 21 de setembro — Foto: Reprodução/Quaest

2. Entre os muito interessados na eleição, Lula aparece com 43% e Flávio com 41% no 1º turno. Os outros candidatos somam 10%. A menos que todos esses eleitores de outros migrem para os dois mais bem colocados, o que não parece razoável, a eleição vai para o 2º turno.

3. No cenário de segundo turno mais provável, Flávio e Lula continuam empatados. O candidato do PL mantém os 42% (na margem pode ter de 40% a 44%), enquanto o candidato do PT oscila positivamente para 41% (podendo chegar entre 39% e 43%).

4. Entre as oscilações relevantes, destaco o movimento positivo de Lula entre as mulheres. Distância Lula x Flávio que era de 3 pontos percentuais na semana passada, foi para 7 pontos nesta semana. Entre homens, situação estável.

5. Mas esse movimento entre mulheres não parece ter acontecido entre beneficiários do Bolsa Família. O anúncio do aumento do benefício pelo governo não funcionou, pelo menos por enquanto, para atrair mais intenção de voto nesse segmento.

6. Flávio mantém sua vantagem numérica ampliando, nesta semana, a intenção de voto entre eleitores de renda alta. Foi um dos maiores movimentos pró-Flávio nesta semana. A vantagem que ele tinha para Lula era de 13 pontos percentuais e agora foi para 20 pontos.

7. Também chama atenção o aumento da vantagem de Flávio entre evangélicos. Enquanto a distância entre os dois continua estável entre católicos, Flávio aumenta a vantagem sobre Lula entre evangélicos de 23 para 30 pontos.

8. Há um indicador que continua projetando esse empate entre os dois principais candidatos. O medo da continuidade do governo Lula continua empatado com o medo da volta da família Bolsonaro ao poder: 43% x 42%.

9. Embora as intenções de voto ainda não tenham se alterado entre beneficiários do Bolsa Família, o medo da volta do Bolsonaro tem aumentado nesse segmento nos últimos 15 dias. Um sinal positivo para os interesses eleitorais do governo.

10. Há dois indicadores que ainda jogam contra o atual incumbente: primeiro, a aprovação do governo: 50% continuam dizendo que desaprovam o governo Lula, enquanto 44% aprovam. Lula precisa de, pelo menos, 46% de aprovação para chegar favorito na reta final da campanha.

11. O resultado só não é mais desafiador para o presidente porque a comparação é com o governo anterior. Na comparação direta, 42% acham que Lula 3 é melhor e 42% acham que é pior do que foi o governo Bolsonaro.

12. A percepção sobre a vida econômica também joga contra o governo. Apenas 10% dos brasileiros afirmam que perceberam um aumento de renda superior ao custo de vida. Para 33%, a renda não aumentou, e 24% dizem que a renda aumentou menos que o custo de vida.

13. A favor de Lula está o percentual majoritário que acredita que ele vá vencer a eleição. É o bandwagon effect — ou “efeito adesão ao vencedor”. Quem parece que vai vencer tende a se expressar mais, o que acaba mobilizando mais gente em volta. Em eleições competitivas, a expectativa de vitória funciona como capital político.

14. A crise do banco Master começa a produzir mudanças de percepção. O eleitorado deixa de criticar todo mundo e passa a ver efeito negativo sobre Bolsonaro (21%), o STF (16%) e Lula (11%).

15. Mas esse efeito é fruto de uma narrativa política. Do lado lulista, aumentou quem acredita que a família Bolsonaro seja a mais afetada pela crise. Do lado bolsonarista, aumentou quem coloca o peso sobre Lula e o STF. Ou seja, a crise começa a produzir narrativas políticas eficazes para mobilizar os dois lados.

16. A crise do Supremo, por sua vez, continua mobilizando eleitores. Embora a maioria diga que seu voto não será afetado pela crise, passou de 22% para 26% os que afirmam que a crise reforça a escolha presidencial atual.

17. Esse aumento, nesta semana, aconteceu especialmente entre o eleitorado de esquerda. Nos demais segmentos, estabilidade. Ou seja, a reação observada depois da última semana é claramente mais mobilizadora para Lula. Detalhe importante: 11% dos independentes estão pensando em mudar seu voto diante dessa crise.

18. A Quaest entrevistou 2.004 pessoas, entre os dias 17 e 20 de setembro; a margem de erro é de 2 pontos percentuais e o nível de confiabilidade é de 95%. Registro no TSE: BR-06004/2026.

articles.title: Quaest: 50% desaprovam governo Lula e 44% aprovam | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisa encomendada pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo mostra também dados sobre avaliação do governo, aumento de preços, custo de vida e principais preocupações dos brasileiros.
articles.summary: Pesquisa encomendada pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo mostra também dados sobre avaliação do governo, aumento de preços, custo de vida e principais preocupações dos brasileiros.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta segunda-feira (21) mostra que 50% dos eleitores desaprovam o governo Lula, enquanto 44% aprovam.

Em relação à pesquisa anterior, de uma semana atrás , o índice de desaprovação não mudou e a aprovação oscilou um ponto para cima (de 43% para 44%).

Desaprovam: 50% (eram 50% na pesquisa anterior)

Quaest: aprovação do governo Lula — Foto: Arte/g1

Quanto à avaliação do governo, houve o índice de percepção negativa passou de 38% para 42%.

Quaest: avaliação governo Lula — Foto: Arte/g1

A Quaest ouviu 2.004 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 17 e 20 de setembro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança de 95%. O número de registro da pesquisa é BR-06004/2026.

Governo Lula é pior ou melhor do que o governo Bolsonaro?

A pesquisa mostra um eleitorado dividido na comparação entre os governos de Lula e Jair Bolsonaro:

42% consideram o governo Lula melhor que o de Bolsonaro.

42% consideram o governo Lula pior que o de Bolsonaro.

A Quaest também perguntou aos eleitores como eles avaliam a economia brasileira e o custo de vida.

66% afirmam que os preços subiram nos mercados no último mês.

Outros 8% dizem que perceberam uma queda nos preços.

31% dizem que a renda aumentou tanto quanto o custo de vida.

24% afirmam que a renda aumentou menos que o custo de vida.

10% consideram que a renda aumentou mais do que o custo de vida.

Quaest: renda e custo de vida no Brasil — Foto: Arte/g1

A violência é apontada como a maior preocupação, com 29%. Na pesquisa anterior, eram 31%. Em segundo lugar, vem a corrupção (21%).

articles.title: Chuva forte causa estragos em Teodoro Sampaio | G1
articles.standfirst: Ocorrências foram confirmadas pela prefeitura e pela Coordenadoria Regional de Proteção e Defesa Civil nesta segunda-feira (21). Não há informações de desabrigados, desalojados ou feridos.
articles.summary: Uma forte chuva atingiu Teodoro Sampaio (SP) no fim da tarde desta segunda-feira (21). Equipes de resgate atendem ocorrências de quedas de árvores e imóveis destelhados.
articles.body:
Uma forte chuva atingiu Teodoro Sampaio (SP) no fim da tarde desta segunda-feira (21). Equipes de resgate atendem ocorrências de quedas de árvores e imóveis destelhados.

Conforme a Defesa Civil municipal, o temporal começou por volta das 17h e durou cerca de 10 minutos, atingindo toda a cidade. A Coordenadoria Regional de Proteção e Defesa Civil também acompanha a situação.

Forte chuva atinge Teodoro Sampaio e provoca quedas de árvores — Foto: Reprodução/Defesa Civil

A Prefeitura de Teodoro Sampaio informou que, em um dos casos, uma árvore caiu sobre um carro. Até a última atualização desta reportagem, não havia informações sobre desabrigados, desalojados ou feridos.

A Câmara Municipal de Teodoro Sampaio foi um dos locais atingidos pelo temporal. Parte do forro e do telhado do prédio ficou destruída. Por causa dos danos, o Legislativo cancelou a sessão prevista para esta segunda-feira (21). Uma nova data deverá ser definida.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: David Almeida participa de caminhada e promete ampliar turismo no Amazonas | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do Avante ao governo do Amazonas participou de caminhada no bairro Zumbi dos Palmares, na Zona Leste de Manaus, nesta segunda-feira (21), onde apresentou propostas para o setor de turismo.
articles.summary: Candidato do Avante ao governo do Amazonas participou de caminhada no bairro Zumbi dos Palmares, na Zona Leste de Manaus, nesta segunda-feira (21), onde apresentou propostas para o setor de turismo.
articles.body:
Candidato ao governo do Amazonas pelo Avante, David Almeida participou de caminhada na Zona Leste de Manaus. — Foto: Patrick Marques/g1 AM

O candidato ao governo do Amazonas David Almeida (Avante) participou de uma caminhada no bairro Zumbi dos Palmares, na Zona Leste de Manaus, na tarde desta segunda-feira (21). Durante a agenda, ele falou sobre propostas para ampliar o turismo no estado e afirmou que pretende investir em diferentes modalidades do setor.

David Almeida disputa o cargo pela coligação "Pra Cima, Amazonas", formada por Avante, Solidariedade, Partido da Renovação Democrática (PRD), Partido Democrático Trabalhista (PDT), Democracia Cristã (DC) e Agir. O candidato é ex-prefeito de Manaus, cumpriu três mandatos como deputado estadual e assumiu interinamente o Governo do Amazonas em 2017.

Entre as propostas apresentadas por David está a ampliação do turismo esportivo, com a realização de grandes eventos nacionais e internacionais. Ele também citou o turismo religioso e o turismo de pesca como áreas que pretende desenvolver caso seja eleito.

“Eu quero trazer para o Amazonas o turismo esportivo, com a Arena Amadeu Teixeira climatizada, trazer grandes eventos a nível nacional e internacional, fazer o turismo religioso, o turismo esportivo da pesca e, sem dúvida alguma, fazer com que a população do Brasil e do mundo possa conhecer o Amazonas da forma que nós conhecemos. Se eu investir em Manaus, eu vou investir no interior, tornar o estado do Amazonas um estado mais conhecido a nível internacional”, afirmou.

O candidato afirmou ainda que pretende ampliar investimentos em estruturas turísticas e levar ações para municípios do interior do Amazonas.

A agenda do candidato começou pela manhã, com uma caminhada no bairro São Jorge, na Zona Oeste de Manaus. Às 17h, David Almeida participou da caminhada no Zumbi dos Palmares. À noite, está prevista uma reunião geral com lideranças no Studio 5, na Avenida Rodrigo Otávio, no Distrito Industrial.

A campanha eleitoral começou no dia 16 de agosto em todo o país. Os candidatos já podem fazer propaganda nas ruas e na internet. Na TV e no rádio, a propaganda começou no dia 28 de agosto. O primeiro turno das eleições será no dia 4 de outubro.

articles.title: Quaest: quem é mais afetado pelo escândalo do Master? | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento divulgado nesta segunda-feira (21) foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo e realizado em meio à crise no STF.
articles.summary: Para 37%, caso afeta "todos" de forma generalizada. 21% citam família Bolsonaro, 16% apontam o STF e 11% mencionam o governo Lula.
articles.body:
Daniel Vorcaro, ex-dono do Banco Master — Foto: Divulgação

Pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta segunda-feira (21) mostra o impacto do escândalo do banco Master sobre a reputação de autoridades, políticos e instituições públicas.

Para 37%, o caso afeta "todos" de forma generalizada. Há uma semana, esse índice era de 46%.

Por outro lado, aumentaram as menções à Família Bolsonaro, de 15% para 21%.

Outros 16% citam o Supremo Tribunal Federal (eram 17% na pesquisa anterior).

11% afirmam que afeta o governo Lula (eram 9%).

Todos: 37% (eram 46% na pesquisa anterior)

Governo anterior e família Bolsonaro: 21% (eram 15%)

Governo Lula e políticos do PT: 11% (eram 9%)

Quaest: escândalo do Banco Master — Foto: Arte/g1

Entre os eleitores de Lula, 46% afirmam que o escândalo do Master afeta negativamente a família Bolsonaro. Já entre os bolsonaristas, 37% citam o governo Lula e 22% apontam o STF.

A Quaest perguntou também aos eleitores sobre a crise do STF e se esse tema pode influenciar a escolha do candidato a presidente.

62% afirmam que não tem influência sobre o voto

26% afirmam que essa crise reforça a atual escolha

A pesquisa foi realizada em meio à crise no STF, intensificada nas últimas semanas depois que o ministro André Mendonça levantou o sigilo de um relatório da Polícia Federal sobre mensagens trocadas entre o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro e um número atribuído ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes . Desde então, vieram a público outros documentos e mensagens — parte deles ainda sob sigilo — com citações a outros integrantes da Corte e a seus familiares.

Na semana passada, terminou sem decisão a sessão extraordinária convocada pelo presidente do STF, Edson Fachin, para discutir o relatório da PF que atribui a Moraes mensagens trocadas com Vorcaro. A sessão foi marcada por embates e trocas de acusações entre os integrantes do tribunal .

Perguntados sobre essa sessão, 74% responderam que já sabiam do que aconteceu na semana passada e 26% não estavam informados a respeito.

A Quaest ouviu 2.004 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 17 e 20 de setembro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança de 95%. O número de registro da pesquisa é BR-06004/2026.

articles.title: Lula e Trump: presidente avalia reciprocidade contra tarifas | G1
articles.standfirst: Em entrevista à CNN, presidente também classificou como 'grave' a ação dos Estados Unidos contra Venezuela, e defendeu realização de eleições no país vizinho.
articles.summary: Em entrevista à CNN, Lula criticou a postura de Trump, ameaçou aplicar reciprocidade comercial e classificou como grave a ação dos EUA na Venezuela.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ) voltou, nesta segunda-feira (21), a criticar a postura do presidente dos Estados Unidos , Donald Trump , em relação a outros países. Em entrevista à CNN, o petista afirmou que Trump "age como um imperador", com a "lei do mais forte", impondo suas regras a outras nações.

Lula está nos EUA, onde participa nesta terça-feira (22) da abertura da Assembleia Geral das Nações Unidas ( ONU ), em Nova York .

"Ele [Trump] age como imperador. É um jeito de governar que eu não concordo. Quando você diz: 'Eu sou forte, eu sou o maior, eu sou o mais rico, eu posso tudo e o restante tem que obedecer'... É a chamada a lei do mais forte, eu não concordo com esse tipo de lei", disse Lula, repetindo crítica feita em 2025.

Apesar de dizer que não concorda com a forma de Trump de governar, o presidente brasileiro disse que fará esforços para negociar a redução das tarifas impostas pelo norte-americano contra produtos nacionais.

Ele lembrou que o Brasil tem um déficit na balança comercial com os Estados Unidos. Em razão disso, Lula tem dito que as tarifas contra exportações brasileiras são "injustas".

O candidato do PT à reeleição declarou que, se as negociações sobre o tarifaço não avançarem, vai avaliar como pode aplicar, de forma concreta, a reciprocidade na relação com os EUA.

"Eu não pretendo entrar em guerra tarifária nem com os EUA e nem com ninguém, eu quero negociar, eu sou de negociação, nasci na vida sindical aprendendo a negociar, então vou tentar todo esforço que tiver ao alcance de um ser humano para tentar negociar", declarou.

"Caso não seja possível porque os EUA não querem, a gente vai ter que tomar atitudes. Tem uma Lei de Reciprocidade aprovada por unanimidade no Congresso. Eu acho que tem produtos brasileiros que os EUA têm muito interesse. Eu acho que é isso que nós precisamos pensar, como é que a gente vai e quais os produtos a gente vai colocar na Lei de Reciprocidade para os EUA", emendou Lula.

A escalada das tensões comerciais entre Estados Unidos e Brasil se intensificou com a imposição de sobretaxas pelo governo norte-americano, que somam até 37,5% sobre diversas exportações brasileiras.

A ofensiva tarifária inclui uma taxa de 25% ancorada na Seção 301 da Lei de Comércio dos EUA, motivada por disputas em torno do PIX, regulação de plataformas digitais e etanol, além de uma alíquota adicional de 12,5% sob a alegação de falhas na fiscalização contra trabalho forçado.

Embora produtos essenciais para o mercado norte-americano, como carne bovina, café e celulose, tenham entrado na lista de isenções, setores de peso como, o do etanol e o de maquinário agrícola passaram a ser diretamente atingidos.

Em resposta à medida unilateral, o governo brasileiro formalizou o acionamento da Lei de Reciprocidade Econômica e abriu consultas diplomáticas para contestar as barreiras tanto em nível bilateral quanto na Organização Mundial do Comércio (OMC).

No entanto, até o momento, o país não aplicou qualquer retaliação prática ou novas tarifas diretas contra produtos dos EUA.

Na entrevista, Lula também falou sobre as eleições no Brasil, previstas para 4 de outubro. Ele disse estar preocupado com o pleito, mas declarou que acredita que será reeleito.

Ele também defendeu as urnas eletrônicas. E afirmou que "tem pessoas que estão condenadas no Brasil e escondidas nos Estados Unidos, tramando contra o Brasil".

"Eu chamo de traidores da pátria. Ele [Eduardo Bolsonaro] é um dos traidores. Está insuflando os EUA contra o Brasil, isso que está acontecendo de concreto. Inclusive com dinheiro, que está vindo pra cá que, logo, vai ser desvendado esse mistério do dinheiro do filme do ex-presidente Bolsonaro", afirmou.

O petista se referiu à cinebiografia "Dark Horse", que está sob alvo de investigações em razão do seu financiamento.

Ainda sobre as eleições no Brasil, o petista disse que os EUA não devem se "meter" no pleito. "Já há indícios de interferência de inteligência artificial. Eu estou muito preocupado com o Marco Rubio porque ele é muito ligado ao pessoal do bolsonarismo, mas por enquanto é só suspeita", declarou.

Na entrevista à CNN, Lula também classificou como "grave" a ação militar norte-americana em território venezuelano. Em janeiro, militares estadunidenses invadiram a Venezuela e capturaram Nicolás Maduro, que, atualmente, está preso nos Estados Unidos.

"É grave o que os EUA fizeram com a Venezuela, é lógico que é grave. Os EUA passam a ideia de que estão governando a Venezuela, todos os documentos que a gente lê, os acordos, os EUA passam a ideia é que estão governando a Venezuela. Ou seja, a soberania do país acabou. Isso não é bom para os EUA, não é bom para a Venezuela, não é bom para a democracia", disse.

O petista defendeu a realização de eleições na Venezuela, para que o povo do país vizinho escolha o seu próximo governante.

"Eu, se fosse a Delcy Rodríguez [presidente interina], convocava as eleições o mais rápido possível para que o povo pudesse escolher o presidente do país. Do jeito que os EUA tratam a Delcy, dá impressão que os EUA mandam na Delcy. O Marco Rubio faz questão de explicitar que ele que manda na Venezuela, que o dinheiro do petróleo vem para os EUA. Esse não é o jeito correto de fazer política internacional ou relação entre Estados. Se Maduro cometeu erro, tem que ser julgado", concluiu.

articles.title: Ex-ministros defendem que STF deve apurar relação de Vorcaro e Moraes, após vídeo de jatinho | G1
articles.standfirst: Moraes e a mulher, Viviane, foram registrados saindo de jatinho do banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, dono do extinto Banco Master.
articles.summary: Moraes e a mulher, Viviane, foram registrados saindo de jatinho do banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, dono do extinto Banco Master.
articles.body:
O Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) não pode deixar de apurar a relação entre o banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro e o ministro Alexandre de Moraes . A avaliação é de ex-ministros do STF, reforçada depois de divulgadas imagens de Moraes e sua mulher usando um dos jatinhos do ex-dono do Banco Master.

Na mesma linha, esses ministros também defendem que as eventuais irregularidades cometidas por André Mendonça sejam analisadas pelo tribunal.

Por enquanto, o tribunal não deve voltar a analisar os casos envolvendo os dois ministros antes das eleições. Pelo menos é o que defendem ministros que apoiam Alexandre de Moraes.

Até quem defende André Mendonça também prefere deixar as análises para depois das eleições para evitar novas cenas "vergonhosas" durante o período eleitoral.

Alexandre de Moraes durante julgamento sobre supostas mensagens de Vorcaro para ele — Foto: Rosinei Coutinho/STF

A sessão desta semana para julgar a petição de Moraes contra Mendonça foi suspensa. Nela, o ex-relator da ação penal do golpe acusa o relator do inquérito do Master de ter agido politicamente e cometido irregularidades para atingi-lo.

Já a petição de André Mendonça pedindo para o plenário apurar as mensagens trocadas entre Vorcaro e Alexandre de Moraes está parada depois que o ministro Flávio Dino pediu vistas. Ele tende a devolver o caso ao plenário somente depois de encerrado o processo eleitoral.

A avaliação é que a crise dentro do STF prejudica mais o presidente Lula e beneficia Flávio Bolsonaro, que lideram as pesquisas de intenção de voto.

Segundo ex-ministros do STF ouvidos pelo blog, varrer para o debaixo do tapete todas as suspeitas sobre as relações de magistrados com o banqueiro seria péssimo para a imagem do tribunal e manteria o Supremo em estado permanente de crise.

Um desses ex-ministros afirmou que tudo precisa ser investigado até para provar quem não tenha praticado nenhum ato criminoso a favor de Daniel Vorcaro.

articles.title: Discord: Governo rejeita proposta e pede proteção urgente de jovens | G1
articles.standfirst: Pedido da AGU enviado à 14ª Vara Federal do DF cita novos episódios de violência e aliciamento, aponta brechas de segurança e cobra cumprimento de exigências do ECA Digital
articles.summary: Discord: Governo Federal rejeita acordo e cobra medidas imediatas contra crimes e aliciamento de crianças, citando falhas graves no aplicativo.
articles.body:
O governo federal, por meio da Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU), reiterou nesta segunda-feira (21) o pedido para que a Justiça conceda uma decisão liminar de urgência obrigando a plataforma Discord a adotar medidas imediatas e efetivas de proteção a crianças, adolescentes e mulheres .

O pedido foi apresentado à 14ª Vara Federal Cível da Seção Judiciária do Distrito Federal após uma tentativa de conciliação.

Segundo a AGU, a proposta de acordo encaminhada pela plataforma foi considerada "insuficiente" por apresentar caráter genérico e não trazer compromissos reais de mudança técnica.

"Dotada de caráter genérico, com exceções e condicionantes dos mais diversos, não é apta a debelar a gravidade dos problemas associados, com a urgência e extensão que a demanda exige. Não há, ainda, compromisso consistente em alteração de arquitetura, aprimoramento de sistemas ou mudança de processos relacionados ao serviço", afirma a AGU na manifestação.

A tentativa de acordo havia sido acertada em audiência realizada no último dia 2 de setembro, quando a justiça abriu prazo de 10 dias úteis para que o Discord formalizasse medidas concretas em temas como verificação de idade, combate à extorsão de caráter sexual, moderação de crueldade contra animais e canal com autoridades no Brasil.

No documento enviado à Justiça, o governo argumenta que o risco aos direitos de menores é contínuo e que a ausência de freios tecnológicos no aplicativo agrava a situação diariamente.

Para exemplificar a urgência, a AGU destacou dois episódios recentes investigados por forças de segurança:

cativeiro em Goiás: No dia 6 de setembro, a Polícia Civil de Goiás resgatou uma menina de 13 anos mantida trancada em um imóvel abandonado em Anápolis (GO). Ela foi aliciada por um homem que conheceu por meio do Discord;

Operação Lívia: Em 12 de setembro, o Laboratório de Operações Cibernéticas (Ciberlab), do Ministério da Justiça, deflagrou junto a polícias civis de múltiplos estados a segunda fase de investigações ligadas a mortes e atos graves decorrentes de desafios virtuais .

A AGU também apontou fragilidades em medidas já adotadas pelo poder público, citando que o aplicativo ainda apresentava brechas para transmissões ao vivo , as lives, no Brasil mesmo após ordem de suspensão expedida pela Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD).

Apenas no estado de São Paulo, segundo dados policiais anexados aos autos, mais de 54 servidores precisaram ser derrubados forçadamente pelas autoridades no último mês.

articles.title: Trump decries Democrats as 'communists,' even as he looks to impress China's communist leader
articles.summary: Communism, President Donald Trump says, is the greatest threat the U.S. has ever faced.  This summer, citing similarly grave concerns, he took the rare step...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Communism, President Donald Trump says, is the greatest threat the U.S. has ever faced.

This summer, citing similarly grave concerns, he took the rare step of delivering a primetime address to the nation , accusing China of "sinister election meddling" in 2020 and reviving his yearslong push to dispute his loss in that year's election.

Even as Trump seeks to decry Democrats as communists ahead of November's midterm elections, he is rolling out the red carpet this week for Chinese President Xi Jinping , the leader of the world's most powerful communist country.

The state visit comes as the president himself has increasingly directed his administration to take large stakes in private companies to try to stimulate the economy — something even some Republicans decry as corporate socialism.

The contradictions between Trump's words and actions risk muddying Republican attack lines on Democrats.

"I do think that we're not offering a clear contrast," said Marc Short, who was chief of staff to former Vice President Mike Pence and worked in Trump's White House in his first term.

Trump and the GOP argue Democrats have moved too far left

During the recent Republican midterm convention in Dallas , the president repeatedly branded Democrats as communists, even proclaiming, "It's going to be a communist country if they win."

"In state after state, the Democrat establishment has been overthrown and replaced by crazed lunatics and radicals," he said, adding, "America has beaten communism before, and we will beat it again."

That's a reference to candidates aligned with democratic socialists who won Democratic primaries in Michigan, Colorado, New York, Florida and Pennsylvania. Trump and other Republicans argue it shows the party is too extreme, although they exaggerate many of the political realities.

It is a way to shift the narrative in the face of a series of drags on the popularity of Trump and his party with Election Day looming. Those include an increasingly unpopular war in Iran , concerns about inflation remaining high and Trump's approval ratings retreating to near historic lows .

Meanwhile, Trump has taken government stakes in private companies

The White House secured agreements giving the federal government stakes in more than 30 companies — including nuclear power producer Westinghouse, metals and element concerns and chipmaker Intel . It has ignored the criticism that this strategy aligns it more with centrally planned economies than capitalist ones.

"If socialism is government owning the means of production, wouldn't the government owning part of Intel be a step toward socialism?" Sen. Rand Paul, a Kentucky Republican and frequent Trump antagonist, wrote on X.

During a recent House committee hearing, Connecticut Democratic Rep. Jim Himes told Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, "I can think of no administration in the last 50 years that is quite as communist as the Trump administration."

The president insists more such agreements are coming. "I will make deals like that for our Country all day long," he posted.

The White House didn't answer questions on whether it saw discrepancies between Trump talking about denouncing Democrats as communists while expressing fondness for Xi and having the government take large stakes in private companies.

Short, the former Pence aide who is now chairman of the conservative advocacy group Advancing American Freedom, said he thinks Republicans are taking "very legitimate attack lines" by painting Democrats as being too far left.

But he said the administration risks "picking winners and losers in the economy" with its private company stakes, as well as with Trump's proposal to send $5,000 to every adult American if the GOP retains control of Congress after November, and his push for price controls on goods such as pharmaceuticals .

"I think those policies, you know, lead to enormous, enormous intervention from the government into the economy," Short said. But he made it clear that he believes the measures don't come close to making the U.S. into a socialist economy like China.

Trump rushed to finish White House helipad in time for Xi

Even as he criticizes Democrats for cozying up to communists, Trump has bragged about his close relationship with China's leader, his chief global rival. When he was in Beijing in May , the president talked effusively about what "an amazing time" he had.

He's not been shy about underscoring that he was building a helicopter landing pad he calls a "work of art" on the south lawn of the White House to impress Xi, while lamenting that his White House ballroom wouldn't be completed in time.

"I can tell you this: It's too bad we don't have the ballroom open," Trump said Friday.

The president also has recalled visiting the Great Hall of the People while in China, and suggested the ballroom might become the "Great Hall of the United States."

Trump's admiration for Xi is part of his fascination with strongmen , said Marc Selverstone, director of presidential studies at the University of Virginia's Miller Center of Public Affairs. Trump has also boasted about his warm relationships with North Korea's Kim Jong Un , Viktor Orbán in Hungary and Russian President Vladimir Putin .

"His interest in strongmen who are communist and strongmen who are not communists," Selverstone said. "That's constant, and playing to them is not unfamiliar to Trump."

Trump criticized Obama for welcoming Xi to the White House

There is often some disconnect between the high and delicate diplomatic stakes of a summit during an election season — as evidenced by Trump himself the last time Xi came to Washington for a state visit.

In 2015, as then-President Barack Obama was preparing to host Xi , Trump — in the midst of his first run for president — criticized the pomp.

"Just take them to McDonald's and go back to the negotiating table," Trump said then, during a rally in South Carolina. He later conceded on Fox News Channel that Xi might at least be worthy of getting "probably a double-size Big Mac."

After he won the presidency, though, Trump's tone has shifted. By 2018, he was even marveling at Xi's position in communist China, remarking that "He's now president for life," during a GOP fundraiser at Mar-a-Lago .

Trump's July speech was critical of China. But that didn't last

Trump briefly appeared to buck his soft spot for Xi in July during his national address when he announced the declassification of documents he said showed a pattern of China interfering in U.S. elections.

"Our elections were left vulnerable to being rigged and stolen," Trump said, without criticizing Xi or calling for penalties against China.

The documents ultimately didn't reveal much new information, or support Trump's claims. And the president has since tried to downplay the alleged election meddling.

"It took place a long time ago. I think China is maybe a little bit different today than it was then," Trump said days after the speech.

Senior administration officials declined to comment on whether accusations of Chinese meddling in the 2020 election would come up during Trump's discussions with Xi. But it's unlikely that the politics of the midterms will have much impact on the summit, said Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on U.S.-China relations at the International Crisis Group.

"President Trump was very quick, in the aftermath of the (July) speech, to focus his ire on the mainstream media, Democrats. He didn't condemn President Xi," Wyne said, further noting that, when it came to Beijing, Trump made it "clear that the U.S. relationship was still on track."

articles.title: Elon Musk is flying under the radar in the Texas Senate race. Republicans want to keep it that way.
articles.summary: The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin.
articles.body:
The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin. He donned an oversized cheese hat , offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest.

In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration.

Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling.

But that financial tide is quickly turning — with Musk's help.

Unlike in Wisconsin, Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people . He hasn't announced plans for any in-person events, or teased — as he did in Wisconsin — that he'd be handing out $1 million checks to voters.

Privately, Republicans say they want Musk to keep his distance. In interviews, more than half a dozen Republican strategists involved in the Texas Senate race say they hope Musk follows his 2024 model of electoral involvement, which led to a Republican sweep of the White House and Congress. Then, Musk spent more than $250 million on Donald Trump and his party.

Republicans believe Democrats will attempt to turn Musk into a boogeyman if he takes on a higher-profile role in Texas or other battlegrounds. One Republican consultant involved in the Texas Senate race said that was the perception in Wisconsin.

"He came in super late, and it was very public," said the consultant, who, like others interviewed for this article, were granted anonymity to speak candidly. "Elon spending money became the story, which I think maybe was a mistake."

A different Republican strategist involved in Texas campaigns said those around Musk learned from the experience.

"Did Elon bring some things to the Wisconsin race that hampered things? Probably," the person added. "But I think they will adjust for that."

Democrats, however, say they welcome Musk more publicly entering the fray in Texas.

"Elon, bring it. You've failed in Wisconsin. You'll fail in Texas," said Nathan Johnson, a Democrat running to replace Paxton as attorney general. "I'm not afraid of Elon bringing his political money here. All these policies favor him or people like him."

An in-your-face Musk campaign would play into Talarico's narrative that the real American divide isn't left versus right but "top versus bottom," with elites and billionaires exerting control over the working class, they say.

"James is running largely on costs and corruption," Luke Warford, a Texas-based Democratic strategist and chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said of Talarico. "The idea of the richest man in the world coming in late to try to buy the election and save Ken Paxton really plays into James Talarico's argument."

The Texas Senate race has all the makings of a contest that would attract Musk. The conservative narrative building against Talarico amplifies his past remarks in support of transgender people, including his comment that " God is nonbinary ." Talarico told Fox News he was being "provocative" and was trying to convey that one cannot use "human categories to define God."

Musk has spoken publicly about his own transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, saying she was "not a girl" and was figuratively "dead." He also alleged that he had been "tricked" into authorizing trans-related medical treatment for her when she was 16. Wilson previously told NBC News that Musk was an absent father who was cruel to her as a child for being queer and feminine.

At this point, Musk's America PAC has not said how much it will invest in Texas, but a person with knowledge of the group's thinking indicated that as of now, the Paxton-Talarico contest was not slotted to receive more focus than other Senate or congressional races the group is investing in across the country, saying "every state and district where we are spending is a priority."

To date, America PAC has spent nearly $5.2 million on digital ads, mail, live calls and pamphleting in Texas, but that number is expected to significantly climb.

In all, the super PAC has spent $14.7 million on congressional races, including seven Senate races and nearly three dozen House races. The group has spent the most money on the Texas Senate race, followed by nearly $3 million on Senate races in Ohio and Michigan.

National Republican groups long knew they would have to provide air cover for Paxton because of an initial fundraising disadvantage to Talarico, who had $21 million in cash on hand compared to Paxton's $1.7 million at the end of June, according to campaign finance reports. Today, a flood of Republican money is pouring in from several sources and the balance has suddenly tipped in Paxton's favor.

"America PAC is working in full coordination with the entire GOP apparatus and is investing in the states and districts that will decide control of the House and Senate," America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo said in a statement. "Our only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington and stopping the lunatic left from bringing us back to the days of open borders, rampant crime, and woke policies."

Paxton's status as a scandal-plagued candidate who has been impeached and indicted — coupled with the fact he's coming off a contentious primary against Sen. John Cornyn and much of the Republican Party establishment, aside from Trump — makes him among the most vulnerable front-line Senate Republican candidates in a state where Democrats have not won a statewide post in three decades.

After Trump's late endorsement helped propel Paxton over Cornyn, groups like the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, were left scrambling. The election cycle budgets were, in part, built on the idea that Cornyn would not need nearly as much national fundraising help.

"Cornyn had his own fundraising machine, he could raise a lot of money on his own, so it was going to make things easier to cover other important close races," said a Republican consultant familiar with the thought process. "I know they [Elon] are focused more on the ground game stuff. MAGA Inc. is on digital and mail. This pretty much turned out the way we thought it would. It's an expensive endeavor and a team and multigroup effort."

The pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC has pumped at least $15 million into TV ads that have included hitting Talarico on previous votes involving China.

So far, MAGA Inc. has spent $10 million in the state to help boost Paxton, its second-biggest single-state investment.

The group did not return a request for comment, but in an interview with NBC News last week, MAGA Inc. chief James Blair said the group had booked $10 million worth of TV ad time in Texas. Blair noted the previous disparity in spending, with Talarico and related groups pummeling Paxton on TV.

"The fact is Ken Paxton had $100 million spent against him in the primary," Blair said. "Talarico had $0 spent against him in the primary, and that has an impact on candidate images that takes time to rectify. But the resources … have begun to be deployed now in earnest [and] will take care of that problem."

A veteran GOP official directly involved in the race contended that the shift toward spending in Texas did not take away from other battlegrounds.

"This spending will not take away from other investments," the official said. "This came from a collection of Texas folks very committed to making sure that seat remains Republican. They see the polling, and that James Talarico is so extreme. No one wants to see Texas turn blue."

When asked about the onslaught of money headed toward Talarico, spokesman JT Ennis said, "Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James because they're scared of the people-powered movement we're building to fix this broken, corrupt political system."

articles.title: Senate Republican on Trump Jr. wedding gift from Russian oligarch: ‘Really bad’
articles.summary: Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) says Donald Trump Jr.’s acceptance of lavish gifts from a Russian oligarch with ties to the Kremlin looks “really bad” and warned i...
articles.body:
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) says Donald Trump Jr.'s acceptance of lavish gifts from a Russian oligarch with ties to the Kremlin looks "really bad" and warned it would be "wrong" for anyone with "proximity to power" to accept items of great value from an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"Anytime someone gives you a $250,000 gift and they have strong ties to the Kremlin, that's wrong," Cassidy told Margaret Brennan, the host of CBS's " Face the Nation ," on Sunday.

"You — with that proximity to power, being the president's son, you've got to give faith to the American people that Washington is not a swamp," he added. "And even though in your mind it might be a gift, the appearance of it is really bad."

Cassidy, however, said Trump Jr., President Trump's eldest son, made the right move by paying back Russian businessman Umar Kremlev.

"And so I'm glad it's been repaid," he said. "It would be nice to have that kind of verified, and, no, it shouldn't have been done in the first place."

Cassidy became at least the third Republican senator to criticize Trump Jr.'s acceptance of tens of thousands of dollars' worth of gifts from Kremlev, the president of the International Boxing Association, who helped pay for a luxurious after-wedding party for Trump Jr. and his new wife Bettina Trump.

ProPublica broke the story last week that Kremlev paid to rent one of two private islands where the Trumps held a three-day party in the Bahamas and also footed the bill for a private fireworks show.

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) on Friday ripped Trump Jr. for taking such lavish gifts from a Kremlin ally, declaring it smelled of "corruption."

"A Russian oligarch paid for a lavish wedding after-party for Donald Trump Jr., which to me just thinks, 'It's corruption,' I don't like it," Curtis said in a video Friday.

"You'll hear more from me later on. This is a big deal," he said.

Bettina Trump confirmed in a social media post that the couple's "dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations" but emphasized it was "AFTER" the wedding itself, which was a private ceremony attended only by family.

President Trump told reporters Friday that his son paid back Kremlev and that he did nothing wrong.

"Well, it's totally allowed, and a lot of people have parties and all, but it's totally allowed," the president said. "But as I understand it, he paid him back. He didn't want to have that, so I hear he paid him back."

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) last week called Kremlev's financing of Trump Jr.'s three-day party "beyond bad."

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), however, said last week he needed to learn more about the financial arrangement.

"I don't know all the particulars on that. I've seen — or heard, I should say — some of the reporting around that. I just don't know enough about it," he said.

articles.title: Critics pounce as prominent Dem senator seems to make admission about party's far-left ‘fringe'
articles.summary: Cory Booker seemed to dismiss Abdul El-Sayed as a "fringe" figure on "Meet the Press," but their recent "warm" D.C. meeting tells a very different story.
articles.body:
Booker emphasized the need for tax cuts and criticized President Trump's economic and foreign policies during the interview.

Political observers noted that Booker's response may indicate a struggle within the Democratic Party to distance itself from far-left candidates and socialist ideologies.

Sen. Cory Booker's response to a question about Abdul El-Sayed's election campaign in Michigan has some online observers questioning whether the Democratic Party's elected officials are behind the socialist-adjacent candidate.

The Democrat from New Jersey joined Kristen Welker on ABC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday, when he was asked a wide variety of policy questions along with a question about President Donald Trump's announcement that he is banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds. But the question about El-Sayed stole the show.

"Senator, you see there in our polls that socialism is viewed even more negatively than the 'MAGA movement,'" Welker began. "President Trump is trying to paint progressives, and frankly all Democrats, as socialists, and we're seeing one of the big battles play out for progressivism in Michigan right now with Abdul El-Sayed... do you think Democrats are drawing a firm enough line between themselves and socialism?"

"Again, this is really what the Republicans want to do — focus on a few fringe people," Booker replied.

He then diverted away from discussing the party establishment's fracture with far-left candidates and pivoted to attacking Trump's economic and foreign policies.

"I serve in the United States Senate and I could go through my colleagues, left and right," Booker said. "What we want right now is to end these reckless tariffs and drive down prices, to end this war to drive down prices, to give a tax plan for this country that puts more money in working peoples' pockets and ends the giveaways to the wealthiest of Americans."

Political observers on X quickly seized on the response, claiming that Booker is too late in the push to try and distinguish the Democratic Party from its far-left fringe and the rise in socialist candidates in this year's midterm elections.

"Oops," radio show host Jason Rantz said simply of Booker's comments to Welker.

"A day late and a dollar short," said Trump Media & Technology Group communications adviser Katie Zacharia. "Senator Booker is trying to disassociate as the 'Big Tent' burns."

She added that the senator should have condemned socialism outright, claiming the "Dem party [is] in disarray."

"I really wonder what the internals they showed those senators in DC said," said author Carl Paulus, speculating that polling within the Democratic Party could suggest that the far left is dragging them down and causing sitting lawmakers to change their tune with just weeks until November's election.

Booker was one of several senators who met with El-Sayed during a trip to Washington, D.C., last week.

After the meeting, led by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., El-Sayed's campaign described the gathering as "warm."

"We're united in the fact that we have to win Michigan. Whatever our difference is, our agreement on the importance of winning Michigan to take back the Senate majority [is] overwhelming," El-Sayed told MS NOW of the meeting.

"We had a warm meeting, good conversation, and I know that we left that conversation committed to doing what we need to do to take on different perspectives. And I also know that the things that bring us together are so much bigger than any of the disagreements that we have."

Fox News Digital reached out to Booker's office and the El-Sayed campaign but did not hear back at time of publication.

articles.title: The 2026 midterms are 6 weeks away. Which party has a better chance of winning? Here's what the latest polls say.
articles.summary: Trump's approval rating is going down. Democrats' lead on the generic ballot is going up. Could this be a "wave" election?
articles.body:
The 2026 midterm elections are just 43 days away. All of the key primaries have been decided . With summer officially behind us, the fall campaign is now underway.

So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to zoom out … and geek out over some cold, hard data.

The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. Big events can, and often do, change the course of elections. And six weeks can be an eternity in politics.

Yet the stakes in November couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too.

The state-by-state midterm landscape is finally taking shape — and a few clear polling trends are emerging. Here are the numbers to watch as Election Day nears.

Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds).

You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading.

At this point in 2022 — after more than a year and a half of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats had a narrow lead (1.3 percentage points) on the generic ballot. Six weeks later, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House .

At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 8 points on the generic ballot. Six weeks later, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House .

Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But six weeks out, voters were starting to break against Democrats. In 2014, a final Republican polling lead of 2.4 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House ; in 2010, those numbers were 9.4 points and 63 seats, respectively .

So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election.

Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — about 8 percentage points , on average — and it has been steadily growing over the last two weeks.

Democrats probably won't reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House.

National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is possible — but Dems are also playing defense in places like Michigan, Georgia and New Hampshire. Here are the 10 races to follow:

What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 8 percentage points . One recent poll shows a tie .

Republican Mike Rogers (former member of Congress)

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (public-health epidemiologist and former Wayne County, Mich. health director)

What the latest polls say : Eight polls have been conducted over the last month. Seven of them showed El-Sayed in the lead, by anywhere from 2 to 5 percentage points .

What the latest polls say : Every poll conducted since July shows Brown leading Husted , with margins ranging from 4 to 8 percentage points.

Republican Mike Collins (member of Congress)

What the latest polls say : Ossoff holds a solid lead over Collins, with the two most recent polls putting him ahead by 4 to 7 percentage points .

Republican Michael Whatley (former Republican National Committee chairman)

Republican John E. Sununu (former U.S. senator)

Democrat Chris Pappas (four-term U.S. representative) What the latest polls say: Pappas and Sununu, who both won their Sept. 8 primaries, have traded leads in recent polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. But the most recent survey, conducted from Sept. 16 to 17, showed Pappas ahead by 8 .

Democrat Mary Peltola (former member of Congress)

What the latest polls say : Most surveys conducted since Alaska's Aug. 18 primary have given Peltola a slim lead ; a mid-September AARP poll showed her ahead by 7. But the most recent sounding suggests this could be a photo finish.

Republican Ashley Hinson (member of Congress)

Democrat Josh Turek (state legislator and former Paralympic athlete)

What the latest polls say : Hinson and Turek have traded small leads in surveys released since Iowa's June 2 primaries .

Republican Ken Paxton (state attorney general)

Democrat James Talarico (state legislator)

What the latest polls say : Nearly every poll conducted over the summer has shown Talarico leading Paxton, though the margins are small — between 1 and 6 points.

Republican Pete Ricketts (incumbent and former governor)

Independent Dan Osborn (veteran and former union leader with Democratic support)

What the latest polls say : Surveys are few and far between. But the most recent results suggest Osborn could be competitive.

Advantage? Too close to call — though Democrats seem to have gained ground over the last two weeks.

Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability

To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle.

At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them.

According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 59% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 39% who approve. That puts the president's net disapproval rating at 20%.

An American Research Group poll released on Monday measured Trump's approval rating at 29% — his lowest mark ever. The same survey showed the president's disapproval rating at 68%.

Again, history can provide perspective . In mid-September 2018, Trump was about 12 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November.

Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 71% disapprove and 26% approve. That's a 45-point gap.

In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection.

articles.title: He spent 11 months inside DOGE. Now he wants to set the record straight.
articles.summary: Tyler Hassen’s initiation into Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, started as a series of tests. The Houston oil executive says he was...
articles.body:
He spent 11 months inside DOGE. Now he wants to set the record straight.

Tyler Hassen's initiation into Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, started as a series of tests.

The Houston oil executive says he was given vague instructions to show up at an unfamiliar D.C. address. He hastily packed three suitcases and flew east, taking an Uber to a building that he soon learned belonged to Elon Musk's SpaceX. He was whisked to a private office, acutely aware that his tailored suit stood out among the hoodie-clad engineers "too locked in" to their laptops to look up. He was ordered to go through the website of the Department of Commerce and, within days, find two to five ideas to present to Musk.

He checked into a nearby J.W. Marriott and told his wife he didn't know how long he would be gone.

Thus began an 11-month stint at the center of a national firestorm - an exhilarating, chaotic and sometimes scary experience, Hassen told The Washington Post, in his first major interview detailing his forthcoming memoir and plans. The memoir, "Inside DOGE: The Real Story From a Senior Insider," which recounts his time working for the secretive cost-cutting group, is the first tell-all to emerge from one of the most controversial periods of President Donald Trump's time in office - a moment Hassen said he would gladly live through again.

"There's this misconception that we all just went in there and didn't really think about what we were doing," Hassen said, speaking virtually from a hotel room in San Diego. "I spent 24/7 thinking about it, waking up at 3 in the morning thinking, 'Am I doing the right thing?' … And I know I did."

At the heart of the book is a split screen: For many Americans, Musk's project was a callous showcase of bending government to a billionaire's will, associated with tens of thousands of federal layoffs, reams of lawsuits, an AI-enabled effort to kill off wasteful contracts and the gutting of the U.S. Agency for International Development.

But Hassen's memoir enters a different vision into the historical record: He portrays a period marked by a clash in worldviews, in which hardcore capitalists are granted unprecedented power to change a system that they argue operates under completely different incentives, logic and norms.

To Hassen, whose pre-government career involved turning around distressed companies, "DOGE was not radical," he writes in the book. It was "not a wrecking ball, but a catalyst."

In conversation, Hassen comes across as mild-mannered, a distant temperament from Musk, who famously brandished a red metallic chainsaw as a metaphor for cutting government waste. A 43-year-old dad with Boy Scout energy, he doesn't cut the image of the nerd-engineer DOGE bro. He spent his entire adult life "hiring, firing, reorganizing and rescuing failing businesses" in industrial manufacturing and the energy sectors - a skill set that appealed to Musk, his longtime deputy, Steve Davis, and Baris Akis, a venture capitalist who served as a volunteer recruiter.

But for years, Hassen seethed with rage over the national debt, now at $40 trillion. He felt angry that the amount the U.S. spends annually just to service that debt is more than the government spends on national defense and many other public benefits.

So he raised his hand - making a cold outreach to Musk through a network of business world connections, he said in the interview, and pressed the point.

"I'm staring at my daughter, who is 5, and thinking about her at 25 with $100 trillion of debt. And I know if we don't do something about it now, we're going to be there ," he said . " We've got to fix it now. "

By its own accounting, DOGE fell far short of the $2 trillion Musk claimed he would save, and an independent report from the Government Accountability Office has found DOGE's own savings figures to be flawed. But Hassen told The Post he believes the effort was a success.

"Did we eliminate the deficit? No. Of course not," he said. "But we made it on the top of everyone's minds, albeit briefly, for a few months, that this deficit is something that we need to fix."

In the book, he argues that "DOGE fit squarely" within a tradition practiced by some Democratic presidents, from Bill Clinton to Barack Obama, who also sought to shrink bloated government. DOGE was different, he goes on to concede, because of its speed, "faster than Washington was ready for and faster than its defenses could absorb."

But Hassen insists that DOGE was not cruel, a word that appears six times in the memoir, often in relation to laying off federal workers. The refrain can read as a plea for reconsideration of an effort he argues was poorly understood.

"In the private sector, there's an understood bargain," he writes. "You're hired to create value. If the value disappears, so does the job. It isn't personal. It isn't cruel. It's the operating system of capitalism."

Government, he argues in the book, runs on a different logic. Value is "presumed," "permanence is the default," and "the moral burden of proofs falls on anyone who questions headcount - no matter how bloated the system becomes."

After the screening process, Musk and Davis deployed Hassen to the U.S. Department of the Interior, a sprawling agency that manages roughly 500 million acres of federal land and property, national parks, and tribal territories. He took the assignment, he wrote, because he knew "very little" about the agency and the challenge was appealing.

Hassen was eventually promoted by Doug Burgum, the wealthy businessman who heads the agency, whom Hassen described as something of a kindred spirit. He became acting assistant secretary of policy, management and budget and stayed on until November - months after Musk himself had left Washington.

During his tenure at DOGE, Hassen says, he put in 14-hour days, working nights and weekends. During the chaotic period he saw his then-4-year-old daughter only a handful of times. He said he relished the minutiae of the job: poring over grants written in what appeared to him to be bureaucratese, dissembling bloated org charts and consolidating departments.

He says he encountered a bureaucracy more labyrinthine and redundant than he could have ever imagined. He caught spelling errors in a project description written by a vendor charging hundreds of millions of dollars, which he saw as proof of a systemic malaise. The contract, he writes, "stopped me cold." (To drive home the point, a photo of the paperwork with the spelling error is published in the book.)

He told The Post he was exhilarated to get deep into the bowels of the bureaucracy and deploy his corporate-honed skill sets to attack a problem that had long troubled him.

During his first week at DOGE, the team met in a sparse conference room on the top floor of the SpaceX offices - empty except for a giant American flag on the wall, "because it reminded us why we are here," he told The Post. "We had billionaires to 22-year-olds who had dropped out of Harvard, all sitting there on our laptops working with public information - trying to figure out how we can help solve this deficit, this crisis that we're in."

As the group grew, the meetings moved to the Eisenhower Executive Office Building. There, he told The Post that he would present to Musk on a weekly basis, receiving the world's richest man's undivided attention. "He has this ability to grasp so many things, from California water to certain contracts," he said. "We would talk about certain departments for 45 minutes - and how can we fix this - and we'd stay until 2 in the morning."

One time, after a particularly grueling session, Hassen said, he had to sneak out of the White House grounds to sleep. "I was so tired," he said.

During his time at Interior, Hassen was almost like a Where's Waldo character, popping up at key moments that caught the country's attention. When wildfires struck California, Hassen made an unusual decision to fly to the state to grill local officials about why the state's largest water plant wasn't running at full capacity.

The image of him at the Jones Pumping Plant in California became one of the first posts from the DOGE X account identifying its members - prompting a flood of hateful messages and threats to Hassen and his family, he said.

When Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico, it fell to Hassen to officially register the rechristened Gulf of America in the Interior Department's Geographic Names Information System - a move that then triggered a broader recognition of the name change on Google Maps and other online directories.

Hassen says he felt the difference in mindset between the public and the private sector every day. "It showed up in the way career staff spoke about 'the workforce' as something apart - almost sacred," he writes. "Until we can say out loud that government is a workforce like any other - noble in purpose, human in composition, and subject to reality like everything else - reform will look like cruelty before it looks like competence."

There is a clear cognitive dissonance between DOGE insiders like Hassen, who saw himself taking on a deeply patriotic project, and many Americans, who according to polls viewed DOGE disapprovingly.

Not surprisingly, Hassen believes the media is one culprit - treating "every reduction as a moral offense" and framing DOGE leaders' demands for accountability as a "cruelty experiment," he writes.

But in the book, Hassen also reflects on how DOGE's failure to communicate hurt its reputation.

Though DOGE was announced with great fanfare - and its website broadcast tallied savings - in practice the project was highly secretive, with DOGE members often showing up in agencies wielding great power before ever appearing on an org chart.

In the six months before the ill-fated cost-cutting effort imploded, its staff gave just a handful of interviews. Two, including one with Hassen, were on Fox News, and he told The Post that he almost backed out. They were done, Hassen writes, only in response to prodding from then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and Katie Miller, the political operative and podcaster who acted as a communications liaison for Musk's effort.

DOGE members were private citizens, fearful of being personally targeted and unfamiliar with the media apparatus that is part of Washington culture, he says. But fundamentally, the DOGE crew wanted to stay completely focused on the mission itself, he writes. The team was well aware that they needed to move with speed, as they might soon be slowed down by lawsuits, Congress or other bureaucratic forces.

"We were there to work. We weren't there to be public figures," he said in the interview.

In the book, Hassen implies that this was, to some degree, a miscalculation. "Once we stepped back, others were happy to define the work for us."

Ultimately, DOGE did lose control of the narrative, leading to a dramatic split between Trump and Musk five months after DOGE began and leaving the project in the lurch. The night of that split, Hassen said, he paced around the Interior Department like a ghost. The next morning, he went to the agency gift shop and bought his daughter a T-shirt that said "Future Secretary of the Interior." He thought it might be his last night in D.C.

Hassen's experience working with AI for the first time at DOGE led him to take a new job leading Zone Frontier, a former cleaning supply firm with a new mission to provide infrastructure and permitting to the data center industry. Musk's longtime lawyer, Alex Spiro, has also joined the board of directors, something Hassen said was a pure coincidence .

He says he hopes the legacy of DOGE will be that the country's most gifted citizens will seek to serve their government. Instead of draining the swamp, he says, he wants to flood it with talent and energy.

"These are some of the best and brightest we have in America," he said of the DOGE team. "I'm honored to be even a part of them."

Faiz Siddiqui contributed to this report.

articles.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico are suing Trump over White House ban
articles.summary: Three news organizations are suing President Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court, demanding that access for their reporters be immediately r...
articles.body:
Three news organizations whose journalists were banned from the White House last week are suing President Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court, demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in a joint statement on Monday. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

CNN had been scheduled to serve as the television pool on Monday. According to Politico , the four other major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — are declining to participate in White House pool duties moving forward in response to the ban.

According to the complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House are retaliating against them for coverage they dislike.

"President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration," the complaint states. "But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting."

The organizations argue that their reporters were not afforded due process and are asking a federal judge to quickly rule that Trump's ban is unconstitutional. The filing cites a 1977 ruling in which the D.C. Circuit Court found that the White House cannot arbitrarily deny a journalist a press pass without due process.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the filing states.

Trump appeared to respond to the lawsuit in a social media post early Monday.

"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America," the president wrote on Truth Social . "It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!"

The White House released a statement on Monday afternoon, saying that access for journalists is "a privilege — not a right."

"The First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool," the statement read. "No President is required to host a hostile operation on the grounds. Access has always been a privilege — and President Trump is applying that rule."

On Friday afternoon, Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post , saying it was not prompted by any particular stories but was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said at an Oval Office event an hour later while explaining his decision to enact "the ban on the free press."

"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories," the president said. "If they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house."

According to CNN , Trump's close aide Natalie Harp showed him clips of media coverage shortly before he announced the ban.

On Saturday, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were turned away from the White House by members of the Secret Service and had their credentials — so-called hard passes needed for access — confiscated.

The journalists — CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett — are listed as plaintiffs in the court filing.

The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the move, saying it violates the First Amendment.

"The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News senior White House correspondent and WHCA president, said in a statement . "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."

On Sunday, Trump posted what appeared to be an AI-generated image of trash bags bearing the logos of CNN, MSNBC (MS NOW's former name) and Politico outside the White House.

The three news outlets are longstanding members of the White House press pool that provides rotating coverage of the administration and travels with the president.

The daily guidance issued by the White House for Monday listed no primary TV pool, identifying Hearst and Real America's Voice as the "secondary" TV crews for the president's events in Washington and his scheduled trip to New York City for the United Nations General Assembly. Trump is scheduled to meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday afternoon.

U.S. presidents throughout history have complained about negative coverage of their administrations. In 2009, the Obama administration sought to exclude Fox News from a series of interviews with a Treasury Department official in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, but backed down when the other major television networks objected.

Trump, however, has continued his adversarial relationship with the media, often referring to the press as the "enemy of the people."

In 2018, Trump administration officials revoked the press pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta after they said that he had interrupted the president during a news conference. The network sued, and a federal judge ordered Acosta's credentials restored .

A similar situation played out the following year when the White House revoked Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's press pass over a verbal argument between Karem and Sebastian Gorka, a former White House aide, at a Rose Garden event. A federal judge ordered the White House to restore Karem's pass .

Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some official events after the news service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In his first event without a network TV pool on Monday, Trump unveiled the White House's new helipad before departing for New York. His remarks were nearly inaudible on the White House video feed . Joe Reberkenny, a White House correspondent for the Washington Blade who was serving as the in-town pool reporter, said he couldn't hear Trump "over the sound of the helicopter."
