articles.title: White House won't back down as attorney predicts how Trump's latest press tussle will play out in court
articles.summary: A First Amendment attorney predicts Trump's White House ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW will fail in court, calling the action blatantly unconstitutional.
articles.body: An attorney at a nonprofit that defends the First Amendment doesn't think President Donald Trump will come out on top in a legal battle with three media outlets he banned from the White House. But after announcing on Friday his ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico — and the resulting lawsuit against him — the White House told Fox News Digital that Trump isn't backing down. "I think the Trump administration will not fare well in court because its action here is blatantly unconstitutional," predicted Aaron Terr, the director of public advocacy at the Philadelphia-based Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE). Trump took to TRUTH Social on Friday to announce that employees with the three major media outlets will be banned from White House grounds over "reporting FAKE NEWS. He said they "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States." DISNEY SUES FCC OVER ‘RETALIATORY CAMPAIGN AGAINST ABC,’ SEEKS TO BLOCK EARLY RENEWAL PROCEEDINGS Terr says that what media outlets report is not at issue. "There's settled precedent that when the White House opens its doors to the press, which it has done, the First Amendment walks in too," Terr said. "So that means the administration can't ban reporters from the White House grounds just because it doesn't like their point of view or thinks their coverage is too negative or critical, and the president in his statements has been crystal clear that this was the exact reason that he banned CNN, MSN, and ... Politico from the entire White House grounds." Reporters and cameramen with the outlets removed their gear and set up on Pennsylvania Ave. over the weekend and this week continued to film live hits from across the street rather than from their usual spots on White House grounds. In response to Terr's assessment, the White House remained defiant about the ban. "The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President’s Oval Office," the White House said. "The lies they smear are a disservice to the American public and tear at the very fabric of our Democracy. They’re completely capable of reporting from directly outside." CNN FIRES BACK AT TRUMP WHITE HOUSE OVER ATTACKS ON REPORTER, CALLS THEM 'BENEATH THE OFFICE' Monday morning, the three news outlets filed a lawsuit against Trump seeking an injunction that would halt the president's ban temporarily, and asking the court to immediately order the restoration of the media members' White House credentials. CNN was scheduled for White House television pool coverage on Monday. Fox News Media, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News, the other press pool networks, announced in a joint statement that they would not take CNN's place. "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting," the pool members said in a joint statement. Additionally, White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) President Jacqui Heinrich of Fox News, released a statement expressing the organization's support of the outlets. "Today’s action revoking access for journalists from CNN, POLITICO, and MSNOW violates the First Amendment," she wrote. "The implications extend beyond these organizations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future." "The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," she continued. "The WHCA calls on the administration to immediately restore our colleagues’ access." TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SUBPOENAS NY TIMES JOURNALISTS IN GRAND JURY LEAK PROBE TIED TO AIR FORCE ONE REPORT Terr said that while nobody has a First Amendment right to report from the White House, he said court precedent established that once a media outlet gains access to the White House, that access cannot be revoked for ideological reasons. "The principle here is that once the government provides access, it then can't condition that access on whether you're expressing a viewpoint that the government agrees with," he said. "It's a broader First Amendment principle that the government cannot retaliate against Americans for protected speech, and that includes revoking news outlets' access to a space open to the press just because the president doesn't like the actual or perceived slant of their report." Terr noted that while there can be bias in media, the alternative of government-controlled media could result in a much worse outcome. "The First Amendment guarantees that reporters are free to cover the news in a way that they think is best, and it's up to the American public to hear what they have to say and decide whether or not to trust them and their coverage of the government and other issues in our society."

articles.title: House Republican signals opposition to using military funds for Trump’s arch

Mike Simpson (R-Idaho), a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee, said Monday that he thinks Pentagon funding should not be used toward the construction of President Trump’s triumphal arch. Simpson told reporters Monday “there’s a lot of things that we need the military funding for — in fact, we’re short on military funding…
articles.body:
Rep. Mike Simpson (R-Idaho), a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee, said Monday that he thinks Pentagon funding should not be used toward the construction of President Trump’s triumphal arch.

Simpson told reporters Monday “there’s a lot of things that we need the military funding for — in fact, we’re short on military funding right now,” according to Politico.

Asked whether he thinks Pentagon funds should be used for it, he said, “If it was my choice, I wouldn’t put any of that money into the arch,” Politico reported.

Simpson’s remarks come after Trump wrote Sunday on Truth Social the plans for the massive triumphal arch bridging Washington and Virginia will incorporate a “top grade military complex.”

“I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch, planned since the Civil War Era many years ago, at the Receptive Circle adjoining the Arlington Memorial Bridge, into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage,” Trump wrote.

The triumphal arch is intended to be a 250-foot-tall structure, which, if completed, would be the tallest such memorial in the world. It would tower over the Arc de Triomphe in Paris and would be taller than the world’s tallest arch, the Monumento a la Revolución in Mexico City.

It would be located along the Arlington Memorial Bridge, the symbolic representation of the reunified U.S., connecting the North and South following the Union victory that ended the Civil War in 1865.

Simpson said he hopes that if the White House decides to go ahead with the arch, “they would come to Congress and ask for an appropriation for it if they’re going to use appropriated dollars to do it,” according to Politico.

articles.title: Trump inaudible at helipad ribbon cutting amid press pool fight
articles.summary: President Trump was inaudible in live footage at a ribbon-cutting ceremony unveiling the new South Lawn helipad at the White House on Monday after major television outlets covering Trump said they would not participate in the TV pool over his ban of three outlets. While Trump was seen cutting a ribbon on the walkway to…
articles.body:
President Trump was inaudible in live footage at a ribbon-cutting ceremony unveiling the new South Lawn helipad at the White House on Monday after major television outlets covering Trump said they would not participate in the TV pool over his ban of three outlets.

While Trump was seen cutting a ribbon on the walkway to a new helipad and speaking with construction workers, his remarks were not audible.

One host on the conservative outlet Newsmax pointed out in their coverage of the event that there was not a microphone because the pool cameras were not present for the event. A microphone from The Hill’s sister station NewsNation was unable to pick up clear audio either.

“This is one example of it backfiring just a little bit,” the Newsmax host noted.

The apparent audio mishap took place hours after Fox News, CBS, ABC and NBC announced they would not participate in the television pool covering Trump after he announced his ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico from covering the White House last week.

CNN was originally slated to be the out-of-town television pool for Trump’s trip to New York City for the United Nations General Assembly.

Earlier on Monday, CNN, MS NOW and Politico announced they were suing the Trump administration after being barred from the White House grounds last week.

“This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the outlets said in a joint statement Monday.

“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the statement continued. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

Trump defended his move in a post on Truth Social, writing that he was not instituting an assault on the free press but rather an assault on the “FAKE NEWS.”

articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is facing strong pushback from critics after posting his condolences for the death of a jail inmate charged in the killing of an autistic man during an ambush. In line with standard practice, the DOC and its oversight partners will investigate the circumstances of his death." The vast majority of social media users who replied to the post took issue with Mamdani not providing more details about the alleged crime. The individual who died was Luis Alberto Lopez Castillo, who faced charges of murder, manslaughter and robbery related to the 2025 murder of 26-year-old Ron Marte, a man with special needs, the New York Post reported. Prosecutors allege Castillo and his accomplice Axel Martinez ambushed Marte in the Bronx’s Starlight Park as he walked home from work, with Martinez shooting him in the chest while Castillo took his cellphone. "I thought somewhere in the beginning of ‘An Idiot’s Guide to Being Mayor’ here’s a suggestion: ‘Display sympathy for the victims; Not the criminals.’" "Didn’t he murder a 26 year old special needs man?" Jewish advocacy group StopAntisemitism posted on X. Mamdani has been outspoken about his efforts to improve safety and living conditions across the jail system and has made several moves he says will accomplish that, including ending 12-hour shifts for correctional staff, addressing the practice of housing people of different ages together, moving to close Rikers Island, and strengthening oversight under the federal Nunez monitoring agreement. articles.body:

“Congress will never support this idiocy, but if you want to know what’s actually unique about Washington, it’s that it’s the only national capital on planet Earth not represented in its own legislature,” the Maryland lawmaker added. “Why don’t we talk about D.C. statehood instead of this arch-imbecility?”

articles.title: Reporter's Notebook: Congress faces a crisis that the 'AI godfather' warns it may not be ready to address
articles.summary: Geoffrey Hinton warns Congress has a year max to act on artificial intelligence, but political gridlock and midterms could delay legislation.
articles.body: To hear estimates about the growing power of AI, one might ask AI chatbots how long it will take Congress to regulate the technology. But you might not need to do that. You could just inquire with your trusty Capitol Hill correspondent. Let’s call this chatbot "ChadGPT." REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS MEETS AI AS FEARS OF HUMAN EXTINCTION JOLT CAPITOL HILL And it truly doesn’t require that much congressional clairvoyance to divine when lawmakers could address AI – despite the forecast of a looming crisis. You just need a little understanding of the congressional parliamentary posture over the next few months. It’s doubtful that Congress will do anything about AI until after the midterms. Or, maybe even early next year. Results of the midterms will likely consume the lame duck session – regardless of which party wins or loses. Plus, lawmakers must fund the government by mid-December. If either the House or Senate flips, it might be March or April next year until Congress returns to AI. It simply takes Congress a long time to accomplish anything. Especially when there’s a change in who runs the place. The Senate is scheduled to meet for the next two weeks. But House Members fled the Capitol last week – a day earlier than planned and two weeks earlier than the original schedule – even as the "godfather of AI" visited Capitol Hill. Geoffrey Hinton is professor emeritus at the University of Toronto. He’s a 2004 Nobel laureate for his work on "artificial neural networks." He proffered a stark warning for lawmakers. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., summoned Hinton to Capitol Hill for a bipartisan, bicameral briefing on AI. Sanders has called for a ban on "superintelligence." Many lawmakers are furious over what’s unfolded with AI over the past few weeks. They want action now. I had a battery of questions for Hinton when he emerged from the briefing late last week in the Dirksen Senate Office Building. We’ve heard that Congress is lagging when it comes to taking action. ANTHROPIC CEO CALLS ON AI INDUSTRY TO SLOW DOWN TECH RACE, DRAWING SUPPORT FROM ELON MUSK, SAM ALTMAN "How much time do lawmakers actually have to get ahead of this before this is a big problem," I asked. "Very little," replied Hinton. "What is ‘a little,’" I countered. "A few weeks? A month?" "Maybe a year," opined Hinton. "But not much more than a year." Sigh. Hinton characterized the incident where AI agents went rogue and hacked another company as a "little Chernobyl." For the uninitiated, that was the epic meltdown of the nuclear reactor in the former Soviet Union in 1986. It’s one of the most extraordinary human-made disasters in history. But some Republican leaders – and House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., in particular – are downplaying potential doom. Especially after President Trump declared on Truth Social that AI concerns were a "HOAX." "Do you remember when AOC [Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.] said, was it climate change? What was her stupid thing? She said, ‘we're all going to be dead in ten years,’" said Johnson. "This is what the President is saying. You're not all going to be dead in ten years. That's a hoax." Johnson isn’t opposed to legislative action on AI. But he’s certainly taking his cues from President Trump. And even though many Democrats and some Republicans demanded that the House remain in session to wrestle with AI, Johnson predicted that the exercise would be moot. REP. TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES "If I called an emergency session today and I brought everybody in the House and said, ‘let's regulate," I tell you, nobody in the room knows yet what that should look like," said Johnson. "We’re going to have steady hands at the wheel on this." But other Republicans harbor more fear of rapid AI development. "What would happen if we created an independent species that became superior to a human species?" asked Sen. John Kennedy, R-La. Shortly after the briefing with Hinton and others, Kennedy went to the Senate floor and implored his colleagues to pass a bill on the spot requiring AI firms to install a kill switch if their agents rebelled again. However, Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., blocked that on the floor. He feared that such a mandate could stifle innovation. "We're going to just put this blanket regulation on the whole economy with no discussion in one fell swoop, on one day, by unanimous consent?" questioned Paul. Paul’s objection stymied the Senate. The Kentucky Republican is sanguine about what’s ahead for AI. But he worries about congressional intervention. "People have feared technology since the beginning of time," said Paul. " I wouldn't put Congress in charge of a McDonald's." Jeffrey Ladish of Palisade Research assesses the risks of new technology. After the briefing, Ladish offered his own foreboding prediction about AI running amok. "How is this allowed to happen? And how do we ensure this never happens again?" asked Ladish. "Because right now, I guarantee you this will happen again. We are not on track for fixing this." Ladish argued that even researchers "don't know how to control it." That’s why some lawmakers insist that Congress must move fast to combat AI – perhaps even treating it as a new threat. "The people who are the greatest innovators and creators in the world in the AI space are warning us of serious danger. So shame on us if we don't listen to them," said Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., is studying for a master’s degree in AI at George Masson University. He says people are skeptical about AI. But he suggests that the public may grow even more skeptical if one party tries to legislate on AI without bipartisan buy-in. TRUMP ANNOUNCES NEW 'AI FORCE,' VOWS TO PROTECT INDUSTRY AS AI CZAR ANNOUNCEMENT NEARS "We need to do it together. Also, if we do it together, Democrats and Republicans are much less likely to try to reverse it when political winds shift," said Beyer. Some lawmakers are already targeting a scapegoat. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, chairs the House Progressive Caucus. He pins the issue on big tech. "This is on a few billionaires who are the Silicon Valley guys who have developed technology they can't even control," said Casar. "What if it's a hospital next? What if it is nuclear facilities next? That should not be allowed." That introduces a wedge into the debate. Some Republicans are increasingly saying that Congress should lay off the industry and let it innovate. But Casar is producing a foil which has bedeviled both political parties: big tech. Don’t forget that we are just six weeks before an election. Democrats are already jockeying for political positions on AI. "The AI safety issue is very real," said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. "That's why it's so irresponsible that Mike Johnson and House Republicans have gotten out of town before sundown." Could another AI catastrophe compel lawmakers to move sooner? Especially since an expert like Ladish suggests it’s just a matter of time? What if the political battle lines are drawn already between Republicans and Democrats? As far as anyone could tell, John Kennedy was the only Republican who attended the briefing last week. And what if there simply isn’t the political will to move during the lame duck? Or, if Democrats flip the House and Senate, do they try to advance something next year – but it’s viewed as partisan and "big government" by Republicans, standing behind President Trump? You don’t need ChatGPT to grasp how challenging this may be for Congress. You don’t even need "ChadGPT." These are just the legislative realities. As Mary Shelley wrote in Frankenstein, the acquisition of knowledge can be dangerous. Especially if who acquired that knowledge is suddenly more powerful than those who built it. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Frankenstein is a tale of unhinged hubris, ethics and ambition. Congress has tried to legislate guardrails for those mortal flaws for more than two centuries now. Those laws are for humans. And whatever Congress comes up with might not matter to AI.

articles.title: Trump move to ban news outlets blows up at White House
articles.summary: President Trump’s abrupt move to withdraw White House press credentials for three news organizations triggered a rare moment of unity among television networks, with several media outlets announcing Monday they would not cover the president’s daily activities while the ban on the trio remains in place. Both Trump and the White House have shown no signs…
articles.body:
President Trump’s abrupt move to withdraw White House press credentials for three news organizations triggered a rare moment of unity among television networks, with several media outlets announcing Monday they would not cover the president’s daily activities while the ban on the trio remains in place.

Both Trump and the White House have shown no signs of backing down on the president’s decision to keep CNN, MS NOW and Politico out of the White House. The trio on Monday sued to have their access reinstated on First Amendment grounds.

Most media and legal observers say the news organizations are likely to succeed in court this week, and their journalists will soon be back on White House grounds.

The episode is perhaps the sharpest and biggest fight yet between the press and Trump, whose battles with the media have been a long-running feature of both of his presidential terms.

The decision to block Politico, MS NOW and CNN from the White House drew criticism not only from the media and Democrats, but from Trump supporters who back the president’s view that the press is biased but disagree with blocking their access.

“I don’t disagree with the president’s concern about some of these outlets, I just think there’s more effective ways to do this,” Sean Spicer, Trump’s first-ever press secretary, told The Hill on Monday.

“And the other thing is the timing of this. On Friday he was having an amazing announcement on prescription drugs that gets to the affordability issue head on, and this obviously just stepped all over that,” Spicer said.

Trump’s Friday Truth Social post banning the media groups “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” caught White House staffers by surprise.

It came with Susie Wiles, the White House’s chief of staff, reportedly not in the West Wing and after top aide Natalie Harp had been showing the president critical news clips and stories from the three outlets he targeted.

The White House Correspondents’ Association and several press freedom groups condemned the move, as did top reporters and anchors at media outlets typically more friendly to the administration.

“I just don’t think this is something we do in this country,” right-leaning CNBC host Joe Kernen said while pressing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over the president’s ban. “You can’t control the press. The press is going to press, the media is going to media.”

Fox News pundit Brit Hume cast doubt on the president’s political calculus, writing on social media that “if he thinks this will lead to more favorable coverage, I think he’s dreaming.”

In an unprecedented move Monday morning, the current chair of the White House TV pool — a group of networks that rotates duties traveling with the president and covering his daily activities — said the pool would not be covering the president during the ban.

The networks — including Fox News, ABC News, CBS News, NBC News and CNN — hours later issued a statement pushing back more forcefully on Trump’s decision saying, “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government.”

“No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” the outlets said in a firm showing of solidarity.

The back and forth is leading to a standoff that is widely seen by political observers as an attempt by the president to distract from other issues such as the Iran war and the economy, which have both been drags on his approval ratings ahead of the midterms.

Republicans are in danger of losing their House and Senate majorities in the fall elections, which would provide Democrats with oversight powers to use on Trump.

It is also happening as Trump lacks a press secretary following Karoline Leavitt’s resignation from her post over the summer to spend more time with her family.

“To me this really gets to the fact he doesn’t have a press secretary and so he’s just unliterally doing this to media outlets he doesn’t like. He needs to hire somebody for that job like yesterday,” said one national Republican strategist. “Eventually, he’s going to have to let those networks back in because the courts won’t allow this.”

In their lawsuit filed on Monday, the three outlets argued the ban “could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.”

A hearing in the case, seeking a temporary injunction allowing the outlets back on White House grounds, is slated for Wednesday afternoon.

“It’s a pretty damn strong lawsuit. My bigger concern is whether the White House will abide by any ruling. A court can say whatever it wants but are journalists going to push past Secret Service to film at the White House?” said Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation.

Trump in a Truth Social post Monday insisted he is “not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” saying he is instead overseeing “an assault on the FAKE NEWS” which he called a “threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

A White House official echoed that sentiment, telling The Hill: “Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President’s Oval Office.”

“The lies they smear are a disservice to the American public and tear at the very fabric of our Democracy,” the official said. “They’re completely capable of reporting from directly outside.”

The ban has led to a tenser-than-usual feeling at the White House among reporters and press staff, those there say.

“Everybody hopes this is over very soon, and there are signs that there might actually be a rapid resolution here,” one White House reporter told The Hill. “I can definitely say there is a fear here that such an attempt to toss all of them out together like he did gives license to lesser forms of discrimination in the future, both under Trump and future administrations.”

The short-term consequences of Trump’s decision to ban the three outlets — and the ensuing coverage boycott by the TV networks — were apparent on Monday.

As the president spoke at a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the South Lawn helipad, he was completely inaudible because a pool microphone was not there to capture his statements.

“So maybe this is one example of it backfiring just a little bit,” Newsmax anchor Bianca de la Garza said as the right-leaning cable channel attempted to cover the event.

“Obviously the ramifications are right here … you can’t hear the president.”

articles.title: Fewer Democrats planning to cast mail-in ballots in midterms: Survey
articles.summary: More Democrats plan to vote in person as President Trump ramps up his attacks on casting mail-in ballots, according to a new poll released Sunday. NBC News’s latest poll shows that 36 percent of registered Democratic voters plan to cast their ballots in person at an early voting site, a 6-point increase from this point…
articles.body:
More Democrats plan to vote in person as President Trump ramps up his attacks on casting mail-in ballots, according to a new poll released Sunday.

NBC News’s latest poll shows that 36 percent of registered Democratic voters plan to cast their ballots in person at an early voting site, a 6-point increase from this point in 2024. Another 36 percent say they will vote at a polling site on Election Day, 1 point higher than it was two years ago. Five percent say they are not yet sure how they will vote or are unlikely to vote at all.

The poll also found that 23 percent of Democrats say they will mail their ballots in the November midterm elections, down from the 34 percent who said the same this time in 2024.

While NBC News conducted its work to compile the poll, the Supreme Court last week blocked Trump’s executive order to impose new criteria through the U.S. Postal Service on mail-in voting ahead of the midterms.

Fewer independents say they will vote by mail in the midterms, at 20 percent compared with 28 percent in 2024. Twenty-eight percent also said they will vote early but in person, a 6-point increase from two years ago. More independents, 37 percent, say they will vote on Election Day, while 15 percent say they are not sure or likely won’t vote.

NBC News pollsters found virtually no changes with how Republicans plan to vote this year compared with the last general election. Sixteen percent say they will vote by mail, 26 percent say they will vote in person and 53 percent will vote on Election Day.

Democrats are not discouraging voters from casting ballots by mail, but Democratic and progressive groups are urging voters to cast their ballots early and in person amid Trump’s attacks and false claims of voter fraud and election rigging, the outlet reported .

Progressives are concerned that even with the hold on implementing the president’s plans for mail-in voting, news about the criteria could create confusion among voters. Democratic National Committee Vice Chair Jane Kleeb told NBC News that the party is “really pushing” for people to vote early.

“Vote early in person. Go to your county election office and vote early in person,” she said voters have been told. “And that this is the best way that we can get Democrats elected is if you vote early in person.”

Trump critics hailed the court’s ruling, with Democrats describing the president’s plan as likely to result in chaos. Kristen Clarke, general counsel for the NAACP, told The Hill’s The Gavel last week that Trump’s plan would have been “simply catastrophic.”

The NBC News survey was conducted Sept. 11-15 and included 1,000 respondents. The margin of error is 3.1 percentage points.

articles.title: Trump approval falls to all-time low in Reuters/Ipsos poll ⁠
articles.summary: President Trump’s approval rating has dipped to a historic low with the midterms only about six weeks away, according to a new poll. In the Reuters/Ipsos poll, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 32 percent, the lowest of his second term and, according to Reuters, a record low for his entire political life. The fresh…
articles.body:
President Trump’s approval rating has dipped to a historic low with the midterms only about six weeks away, according to a new poll.

In the Reuters/Ipsos poll , Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 32 percent, the lowest of his second term and, according to Reuters, a record low for his entire political life. The fresh approval rating marks a 15-point slide from the 47 percent approval rating he had at the beginning of his second term in the same poll.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll also pegged Trump’s disapproval rating at 66 percent, up 25 percentage points from the start of his second White House stint .

Trump’s low approval rating comes as the president and Republicans are facing rocky political territory in the form of the unpopular Iran war and concerns around issues like the economy and immigration as control of Congress hangs in the balance this November.

In a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was 38.8 percent Monday evening, while his disapproval rating was 59.7 percent.

A recent New York Times/Siena University poll also found Republicans trailing Democrats on the issues of immigration, healthcare and the economy.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll took place Sept. 17-20 among 1,277 people and had 3 percentage points as its margin of error.

articles.title: Austin officials condemn ICE shooting of Venezuelan man, call for independent investigation
articles.summary: Austin City Council members spoke out against ICE after an agent shot a man on Sept. 20.
articles.body:
AUSTIN (KXAN) — Austin officials issued statements against Immigration and Customs Enforcement after an agent shot a Venezuelan man Sunday afternoon.

Neither local law enforcement agencies or the Department of Homeland Security have identified the man yet. Austin immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said the man is her client, and identified him as 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez.

Homeland Security Investigations is leading the investigation, along with assistance from the FBI, according to a DHS social media post . The agency, which didn’t name Garces Perez in its post, said he has a “final order of removal” after he “illegally entered our country under the Biden Administration.”

The agency also said his condition is stable and that he is in federal custody pending removal.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said she did not know why Garces Perez was targeted by ICE and could not speak to his immigration status.

Austin mayor Kirk Watson said the Austin Police Department was not involved in the shooting, but officers did assist in traffic control. Watson said in a press conference shortly after the shooting that he was angry, but “not surprised” about the incident due to similar ICE-related activity across the country.

“With the nature of ICE and the way ICE is doing its business these days, there’s no reason for us to be surprised by it,” Watson said.

Watson joined other Austin City Council members in calling for an independent investigation of the shooting.

“APD would be in a position to offer clear third-party eyes and expertise and allow for a level of independence in an investigation like this,” he added. “From my perspective, the credibility of ICE doing some form of investigation just by itself and excluding others would not be appropriate.”

Several city council members have spoken out against the shooting, expressing outrage and called for ICE to leave Austin.

“The people of Austin deserve answers, and we demand full transparency and accountability,” said council members Vanessa Fuentes (District 2), Jose Velasquez (District 3), and Mayor Pro Tem Jose “Chito” Vela (District 4) in a joint statement . “No federal agency is above scrutiny when the safety and right of our community are at stake.”

KXAN spoke to council members Zo Qadri (District 9) and Mike Siegel (District 7) near the scene of the shooting Sunday.

Qadri called for the release of dash and body camera footage.

“I’m disgusted by what I’ve heard, what we’ve seen happen here in Austin and we’ve seen it happen throughout the country,” Qadri said. “Having it happen in our backyard is just horrifying.”

“Our top demand needs to be that the city can investigate this crime, can investigate what happened alongside the federal government,” Siegel said. “I want folks to know that their city government is doing everything they can to create justice in this situation, to provide safety for the community.”

Council member Krista Laine (District 6) said in a statement that she wishes for Garces Perez’s “speedy recovery” and thanked the first responders on the scene.

“I stand with those demanding a full independent investigation and immediate release of body cam footage,” Laine said. “This blatant abuse of power must be stopped and those who do harm must be held accountable.”

Council member Marc Duchen (District 10) posted a statement on social media condemning the “tactics” ICE has previously deployed.

“ICE has a clear obligation to cooperate with the Austin Police Department and other officials as the investigation move forward,” Duchen said.

Austin Police chief Lisa Davis said her department is working alongside the Texas Rangers in its investigation.

Travis County District Attorney Jose Garza’s office released a statement Sunday that called for an independent investigation.

A member of our community was shot by an ICE agent this afternoon. It is critical that all the facts come to light and that an independent investigation be completed. We are requesting that the Austin Police Department and our office, the Travis County District Attorney, be co-equal partners in the investigation. We further request cooperation from the federal government in giving us access to the evidence. As has occurred in other jurisdictions, it is possible that this incident included violations of state law.

Democratic U.S. Rep. Lloyd Doggett, who represents the district where Garces Perez was shot, issued the following statement:

While we do not yet have all of the facts about today’s alarming shooting, we do have the facts about ICE, which has recently accelerated its intrusion into our community. And our lack of facts results from ICE secrecy and non-responsiveness. Instead of focusing its work on those who may pose a danger to our neighbors, ICE is eager to fulfill a deportation quota by rounding up any immigrant that it can find, including those who are making a real contribution to our community.

Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, is another of Austin’s congressmembers. He said Sunday that he’s asked DHS to cooperate with an independent investigation into the shooting and demanded the agency brief Congress by Sept. 28.

articles.title: Rogers calls for end to war in Iran: ‘Michigan families can’t afford to wait’
articles.summary: Former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.), the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, on Monday said “Michigan families can’t afford to wait” for the Iran war to reach its conclusion, calling for an end to the conflict. Rogers released a campaign ad on the social platform X showing him at a grocery store. He said that Michiganders…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.), the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, on Monday said “Michigan families can’t afford to wait” for the Iran war to reach its conclusion, calling for an end to the conflict.

Rogers released a campaign ad on the social platform X showing him at a grocery store. He said that Michiganders are struggling with rising prices as a result of the conflict and that prices must go down.

“The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly,” he continued. “When it does, energy costs will plummet. But Michigan families can’t afford to wait for that to happen. We need to do something now.”

Rogers proposed suspending the state and federal gas tax of 70 cents a gallon and called for a temporary embargo on American diesel exports until the conflict is over. An increase in supply going to farmers and truckers will put “downward pressure” on the price of diesel.

“Diesel fuels the trucks that bring groceries to this store. It fuels the tractors that grow our food,” he said. “And when diesel costs more, it costs more to grow it, ship it, dock it and ultimately buy it.”

The Michigan Republican’s call to end the conflict follows Rep. Ashley Hinson’s (R-Iowa) remarks on X about how Iowans “shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran.”

Hinson, the nominee for Senate, called for suspending the gas tax, pausing diesel exports, loosening restrictions on gas with higher blends of ethanol and instituting a “diesel relief program to help our farmers and truckers being crushed by high costs.”

She noted that these measures should be implemented “ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.”

Iran’s effective shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world’s oil is exported, has led to sharply rising gas and diesel prices. The national average for gas reached $4.48 as of Monday, $1.30 higher than last year’s average, according to AAA. The average for diesel costs $6.51 per gallon as of Monday.

Republicans have clashed over how to improve their weak polling numbers on the economy ahead of the midterms. Some GOP lawmakers approve of President Trump’s proposed idea to send out $5,000 dividend checks to American adults if the Republicans keep their control of Congress, with Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) saying he would introduce a bill to do so.

But others have warned of the cost of that proposal and are calling for legislation that can alleviate concerns over high prices more quickly.

The president has said the conflict will not end before the midterms and that he is deciding on his next steps , including “ wiping Iran out , letting them rot economically or making a deal,” Fox News reported Sunday.

articles.title: Rep Eric Burlison: 'Most of my colleagues' are 'drunk on spending other people's money, even Republicans'
articles.summary: Eric Burlison (MO-7) has a plan to fix healthcare for the American people, and blames exploding healthcare premiums for Americans' lack of discretionary income.
articles.body: Facing a national debt that has exploded past $40 trillion, Missouri Rep. Eric Burlison isn't holding back on his own colleagues — accusing Washington lawmakers on both sides of the aisle of being "drunk on spending" while working-class families pay the price. Burlison recently sat down for an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital to discuss fiscal prudence, healthcare, inflation, and how Republicans can lift their fortunes ahead of midterm elections just six weeks away. CONGRESSMAN ERIC BURLISON: IN THE BIDEN ADMINISTRATION, 'THE INMATES ARE RUNNING THE PRISON' "Most of my colleagues like to spend money…they like to spend other people's money. They're drunk on spending other people's money, even Republicans, unfortunately, and there's few people up here like myself who were willing to make significant spending reductions. "And so we had to fight tooth and nail to get any spending reductions in the Big, Beautiful Bill. And we were demonized by the left, obviously, but we had to fight members even on our own side of the aisle to make those spending reductions. "But, look, at some point, the party is going to be over, and we are all gonna wake up in a drunken stupor with a hangover, and it's going to be painful, and we're going to have to figure out how to get our way out of that. "All of these sins of overspending are haunting us. And now we're seeing…inflation that we can't control. We're seeing the interest rates go through the roof. At some point, you can't keep borrowing money…Sadly, my colleagues that weren't willing to cut spending are going to be forced to cut spending." Despite seeking to portray themselves as the party of affordability, the GOP seems to have a major messaging problem as it heads into the tumultuous midterm elections. Burlison points to healthcare as the main problem: "I mean, again, it's really sad. This office has been broadcasting to the leadership every chance that we can that the American people are feeling the crunch, they're feeling the affordability crunch. We put together a solution that we call the Great American healthcare plan. We also have another bill that addresses the housing affordability issue. "This office has been doing everything we can to try to fix the affordability issue and have been putting these ideas and solutions in the faces of leadership for at least two years. It's just unfortunate that we can't get people to do the difficult things. And sadly that's because Washington DC doesn't like to do difficult things and fixing healthcare is the number one thing that we should be looking to do. WE'RE MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE FREEDOM CAUCUS. THE US MUST CHOOSE: EITHER $20 TRILLION IN DEBT OR MEDICAID REFORM "Healthcare cost is eating away everyone's discretionary dollars…In the year 2000, the average American family was paying $6,000 a year for insurance premiums for a family of four. Today, that's $27,000 a year. If that had followed normal inflation, that would only be $11,000 per year. "So if you ask the average family of four, would you like to be paying health insurance premiums at $11,000 a year, they would say, heck, yeah, that sounds like a great deal. That is not what they're paying today. They're paying $27,000. So if you think about that, just that alone, that is crowding out everything else that the average American family has to pay. You have to come up with another $16,000 that you didn't have to come up with before, in order to pay for a healthcare system that has exceeded inflation by three-fold. "So three times normal inflation for the healthcare premiums, health insurance premiums. It's not sustainable, and it's crowded out everything else, and it is the reason why young people cannot afford to buy a home. It's the reason why people have a hard time going out to eat. It's a reason why people aren't going on vacation as much. People are having to make very difficult choices, and it's not the same choices that people had to make 20 years ago." As Elon Musk and DOGE-fervor swept across the nation's capital at the beginning of 2025, Burlison's initial enthusiasm soon turned to disappointment as he saw colleagues avoid much-needed spending cuts: "DOGE was the most exciting thing I've ever seen in politics. And I was super excited about it. But I also was skeptical. I watched Elon come give speeches to my colleagues. And what was ironic is that some of the most swampy members of Congress were rushing to the microphones to embrace Elon to talk to him to tell him where he should go to look for spending reductions. "And yet those very people were the ones that were voting against every spending reduction that you would ever bring to the floor. We've had hundreds and hundreds of opportunities to cut spending… We submitted hundreds of amendments to the appropriations committees to cut spending and yet each and every time, anytime there's ever a vote to cut spending, they fail. "So, look. All we have to do as Republicans is look in the mirror and say where's the problem? It's me, it's us…I'm one of these almost going extinct members of the Republican Party that still believes in fiscal prudence, still believes and in cutting spendings this small government free market conservative. But unfortunately, that's not how all of my colleagues feel." Burlison argues that the GOP has a fundamental messaging problem and has urged his colleagues to zero in on their economic pitch to the American public, with a particular focus on the healthcare crisis: "So, in my opinion, it's not enough to run against a platform. If you have to provide a vision to the American people, and if you ask the American voter today, what will the Republican Party do if they're reelected…I don't think that they would know. And so to me, the vision that I would provide is to say, 'we're going to fix healthcare. We're going to make healthcare affordable. We're gonna to make it a free market. The prices are going to be transparent, and you're going to know exactly what you're buying'." Finally, Burlison has a quick prescription for bringing down pain at the pump tied to the engagement in Iran: CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP "Well, conservatives, we love cutting taxes and I think that we should be cutting the fuel taxes during this period of time. I would love to eliminate the taxes altogether, but at least it would make sense that during this conflict that we should cut taxes on both gas and diesel until this war is resolved. "I think that that would have a pretty good impact on people's pocketbooks. I mean you're talking for diesel that would be 40 cents a gallon. That's, that's pretty significant."

articles.title: Trump and the GOP lose a key edge with voters: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into our newest poll to underscore the challenge facing Republicans at the polls this fall. Plus, Natasha Korecki and Matt Dixon examine Elon Musk’s under-the-radar midterm role (so far). — Adam Wollner Trump and the GOP lose a key edge with voters Analysis by Sahil Kapur Ever since he first descended down a golden escalator in 2015, President Donald Trump and his party have possessed a powerful political asset: Voters have generally trusted them on the economy. But that appears to be shifting heading into the November midterm elections.Our new NBC News poll released over the weekend found that 39% registered voters trust Democrats more to handle the economy, compared to 38% who trusted Republicans more — a 1-point difference. While voters have been split relatively evenly on the issue between the two parties in recent NBC News polling, Republicans had long held an edge on the question. Republicans had a 15-point advantage in October 2018 — one month before Democrats gained a net of 41 seats to win control of the House — and a 19-point advantage in September 2022. The only other time during the Trump era Democrats led on the question of which party voters trust more on the economy was in December 2017. [chart] Similarly, the latest NBC News poll showed that 55% of registered voters said that Trump’s policies have “hurt” the economy, while 26% say they’ve “helped.” That net margin of negative 29 points is 16 points worse than Trump performed on the issue in a March NBC News poll. And in September 2018, voters said 41%-26% that Trump’s policies had helped the economy, rather than hurt. Inflation and the cost of living topped the list of voters’ most important issues facing the country in the new poll (28%), while another 9% said jobs and the economy. The issue of the economy has powered Trump in his own presidential bids. Most recently, in 2024, 53% of voters said they trusted Trump more to handle the economy, according to exit polls, while 46% chose Kamala Harris. That year, voters who rated the economy as their No. 1 issue preferred Trump over Harris by an eye-popping 81%-18%. But two years later, voters have soured on Trump and the GOP amid the ongoing Iran war and stubbornly high prices at the gas pump and grocery store. It’s deprived the party of an asset that has tended to shield them even when the chips were down, heading into an election where they are trying to hang on to control of both chambers of Congress. 🗳️ More from the NBC News poll: Voters recoil at candidates who back data center construction, by Scott BlandFewer Democrats plan to vote by mail in the midterms, by Jane C. Timm Elon Musk is flying under the radar in the Texas Senate race. Republicans want to keep it that way. By Natasha Korecki and Matt Dixon The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 Wisconsin Supreme Court race. He donned a cheesehead, offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest. In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration. Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling. But that financial tide is quickly turning — with Musk’s help. Unlike in Wisconsin, Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. He hasn’t announced plans for any in-person events. And privately, Republicans say they want Musk to keep his distance. In interviews, more than half a dozen GOP strategists involved in the Texas Senate race say they hope Musk follows his 2024 model of electoral involvement, which led to a Republican sweep of the White House and Congress. Then, Musk spent more than $250 million to boost Donald Trump and his party. Republicans believe Democrats will attempt to turn Musk into a boogeyman if he takes on a higher-profile role in Texas or other battlegrounds. Read more → 📊 Survey says: A new NBC5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group poll on the Texas Senate race showed James Talarico at 46% and Ken Paxton at 43%, within the survey’s margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Another 8% of potential voters were still up for grabs. Meanwhile, in the Texas governor’s race, the poll found GOP Gov. Greg Abbott at 48% and Democrat Gina Hinojosa at 41%. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.summary: President Trump railed against the judge who has been assigned to a case seeking to challenge his ban on three media outlets from covering the White House and telegraphed he might be forced to let the journalists working for the trio back in the building. “They have drawn a great Judge, for them,” Trump said…
articles.body:
President Trump railed against the judge who has been assigned to a case seeking to challenge his ban on three media outlets from covering the White House and telegraphed he might be forced to let the journalists working for the trio back in the building.

“They have drawn a great Judge, for them,” Trump said of U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who oversaw the White House’s temporary ban on a press credential belonging to former CNN reporter Jim Acosta during Trump’s first term. “In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”

The Oval Office, Trump continued in his Truth Social post , “should be treated with Decorum, Respect, and Dignity, not defiled by Third Rate Clowns, who purposefully distort, twist, and degrade with everything they write or publish.”

Trump last week banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from covering the White House for what he called publishing “fake news” — a matter of national security, he argued.

The outlets sued on First Amendment grounds Monday, with a number of press freedom groups and each of the major news networks voicing solidarity with the three media outlets in response to the ban.

The TV pool typically covering the president on a daily basis did not travel with Trump on Monday in response to last week’s ban, which resulted in a number of reporters having their credentials revoked over the weekend.

First Amendment attorneys and media observers expect the news outlets to succeed in court, while the episode highlights Trump’s ongoing war with the press dating back to his first term.

“Why should I have to give ‘access’ to such people? Perhaps Judge Kelly could explain that,” Trump wrote in his post. “In any event, I have an obligation to fight for the Success and Safety of our Country. FAKE NEWS IS A THREAT TO DEMOCRACY, and I will do whatever is necessary to make sure that the U.S.A. thrives.”

A hearing in the case is slated for Wednesday afternoon.

articles.body:
NEW YORK — President Trump offered rare praise of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) Monday, saying he has “great potential.”

The two leaders chatted inside Gracie Mansion before holding a press conference ahead of Tuesday’s United Nations General Assembly in the city.

“No, I certainly hope he will be a great mayor,” Trump said when asked about Mamdani. “You have to understand — I want what’s good for New York. I want what’s good for the country.”

“So, if I had a choice of having him be a bad mayor or horrible mayor, I don’t want that,” he continued. “I want him to be a great mayor, and he’s certainly got potential and great potential.”

Trump earlier Monday said Gracie Mansion is one of his “favorite places in the World.”

“I spent lots of hours there over the years, with some great Mayors, some average Mayors, and some bad Mayors,” he wrote on Truth Social. “It will be interesting to see how it looks now, invited by Mayor Mamdani.”

He added that was looking “forward” to Monday’s visit.

Trump had repeatedly hit the democratic socialist mayor over his left-wing politics in the lead-up to the election last year.

He and Mamdani met in the Oval Office later that month for a meeting that was more cordial than most expected.

Since then, the president has been critical of some of Mamdani’s policies, accusing him of “destroying” the city with his new proposed tax on second homes.

articles.title: Appeals court reinstates GOP House map in Missouri for November election
articles.summary: A federal appeals court reinstated the Missouri GOP’s 7-1 House map to be used in time for the November elections, delivering a boost for several Republican candidates who wanted a more favorable map for the party to be used in the midterm elections. The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled on Monday that using…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court reinstated the Missouri GOP’s 7-1 House map to be used in time for the November elections, delivering a boost for several Republican candidates who wanted a more favorable map for the party to be used in the midterm elections.

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled on Monday that using an older set of maps that gives Republicans a 6-2 advantage in the House instead of newer ones the party passed last year and used in this year’s primaries was unconstitutional.

“If the 2022 map is used in the November 2026 general election, some Missouri voters will have more say than others on who represents them in Congress,” the circuit court’s panel wrote in its Monday ruling.

The ruling offers a temporary victory for Republicans who are looking to add pickup opportunities in the House ahead of November, though the decision is all but certain to be appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Monday’s ruling to reinstate the 7-1 congressional map does not immediately take effect, however. The federal circuit court gave a one-week pause for the high court to hear an expected appeal to the case.

“If the Supreme Court has not stayed or otherwise altered the permanent injunction by that time, Secretary Hoskins and all others bound by this judgment must fully implement the 2025 map for the November 2026 general election,” the circuit court wrote.

The dispute centers around two different congressional map designs. The Missouri Supreme Court has ordered state officials to proceed with a GOP-favored 6-2 map after ruling that a new 7-1 design could not be enforced unless voters approved it in a referendum.

The new lines had already been used in this year’s primary elections, and state Republicans warned that changing them for the general election would create confusion among voters.

Those concerns were persuasive to U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump appointee, who sided with plaintiff Rep. Bob Onder (R-Mo.) in a separate, federal lawsuit and told the state to keep implementing the new map for November.

The U.S. Supreme Court stepped in shortly after and halted Clark’s order, however. There were no noted dissents, and the justices did not publicly explain their decision.

That left the appeals judges grappling with how to interpret the high court’s ruling, with at least one giving the impression during oral arguments earlier this month that there was more work to be done on the merits.

The 8th Circuit Court reiterated these concerns over voter confusion, writing in its Monday ruling that “any confusion stems from the last-minute decision by a state court to switch the congressional map.”

The issue is now likely headed back to the U.S. Supreme Court for a third time in as many weeks.

The multiple lawsuits and dueling directives have caused havoc for the state’s election officials, voters and candidates, particularly as Saturday was the deadline to send overseas and military ballots. State officials were operating under the assumption that Missouri would be using its old 6-2 map for the general election.

articles.title: Fury erupts over Mamdani parade invite as old Columbus insult resurfaces: ‘Are you kidding me?’
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani's Columbus Day Parade invitation sparks fury among Italian Americans over his 2020 post flipping off a Christopher Columbus statue.
articles.body: A decision to invite New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to Manhattan’s annual Columbus Day Parade has sparked backlash among some Italian-American leaders. The Columbus Citizens Foundation, which is responsible for holding the parade, invited Mamdani in the hopes of fostering a better relationship between City Hall and the Italian-American community, the New York Post reported. Mamdani’s past criticism of Italian explorer Christopher Columbus, however, has sparked backlash among Italians who feel inviting the mayor is in poor taste. "Are you kidding me? This is a WEAK and FECKLESS move by the organizers," Italian American Civil Rights League president Mike Crispi wrote on X. "Zohran has showed contempt for our people and kissing a** won’t change his true feelings. Italian Americans need to wake up and get tough. It’s the only way to preserve our culture." Crispi’s criticism was a reference to a 2020 social media post where Mamdani posted a photo of himself brandishing his middle finger at a statue of Columbus with the caption "take it down." Columbus holds a near-legendary status among Italian Americans, with the 15th-century explorer viewed by many as a historic link between their heritage and the United States. 'DIE HARD' ACTOR ROBERT DAVI BLASTS MAMDANI AFTER NYC MAP OMITS LITTLE ITALY "We feel cooperating is always the better path . . . and we hope to create a good relationship with his office," Columbus Citizens Foundation president Christopher Loiacono told the New York Post when asked about his decision to invite Mamdani. "We hope he will be more open to [working] with the Italian community." It is unclear if Mamdani has accepted the invitation to the parade. articles.title: U.S. military leaders divided over action against the Houthis
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — U.S. military leaders are divided on whether President Donald Trump should get involved with the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to two U.S. officials.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — U.S. military leaders are divided on whether President Donald Trump should get involved with the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to two U.S. officials. The Saudis have been asking Trump for the U.S. military to take action against the Houthis, a request that grew more urgent in recent days as the rebels claimed they shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet and were quickly advancing on Marib province, which is home to Yemen’s largest oil and gas fields. Some military leaders are making the case within the Pentagon and to Trump administration officials that opening another military front in the region is a bad idea amid concerns about the Pentagon’s dwindling supply of defensive and long-range weaponry, while noting that the Houthis are not striking U.S. ships, the U.S. officials said. Yet other military leaders are arguing in favor of strikes, saying the U.S. should help Riyadh retaliate for Houthi strikes in Saudi Arabia and the claim of downing of the F-15 — a challenge to Saudi air superiority over Yemen, the officials said. They said these military leaders are privately expressing concern that for the U.S. not to act more forcefully is a betrayal of an important regional ally. Trump had ordered strikes against the Houthis to begin around 5 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on Sunday, but the military was notified shortly after 2 p.m. on Sunday that the order was canceled, the two U.S. officials said. One of the officials said Trump has not taken military action off the table in the future. One senior U.S. military leader in the region specifically warned that action against the Houthis could create unmitigated risk to U.S. troops in Middle East and the Iran war mission, including a U.S. naval blockade and security operations in the Strait of Hormuz, the two U.S. officials said. They said the military leader also made clear that U.S. forces could carry out the Iran mission and strikes against the Houthis and mitigate some of the risks, the officials said. The internal divide underscores the bind the president is increasingly in as the U.S. remains locked in a war with Iran that he began but has struggled to end, and faces a shortage of key weaponry. The Saudis have been a critical U.S. ally in the Middle East, including throughout the war with Iran. Trump told Fox News over the weekend that he’s deciding whether to escalate the war with Iran, a position he has articulated on and off over the past few months. The White House and a spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in Washington, D.C., did not respond to a request for comment. The Pentagon declined to comment. There has already been tension between the U.S. and its Middle East allies over the war. In May, Saudi Arabia was surprised by an announcement by Trump to help ships through the Strait of Hormuz and suspended the U.S. military’s ability to use its bases and airspace. Trump abruptly reversed his decision. The U.S. has already been supporting the Saudis by sharing intelligence, helping with planning, sending military advisers forward with the Saudi forces and even providing some logistical support, NBC News has reported. But the Saudis have repeatedly asked the U.S. to do more, including help with strikes against the Houthis. Trump had not shown interest in acting until Thursday, when Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman told him in a phone call that the kingdom cannot succeed alone and after a series of developments — including the Houthis targeting Saudi infrastructure, downing the F-15 and threatening to take control of Yemen’s oil industry, according to one of the U.S. officials. After the call, Trump ordered the military to provide him with fresh options for strikes against the Houthis, the official said. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Dan Caine called a 6 p.m. emergency meeting in The Tank, the top-security conference room in the Pentagon, to discuss options, the official said, canceling a trip to Copenhagen to meet with NATO chiefs of defense. U.S. military officials have presented Trump with options for degrading Houthi military capabilities and stopping the rebels’ recent advances several times since Thursday, the official said, adding that the Pentagon has enough assets in the region to be ready to act if ordered to do so. The New York Times reported some details of Trump’s decision-making process. Violence escalated over the weekend, as the Houthis said they’d used missiles and drones on Saturday to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh and an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub. The spokesperson for the coalition forces issued a statement on Saturday saying Saudi Arabia had successfully intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh and that the Houthis “target civilians and civilian infrastructure in the capital.” The militant group also made a rapid advance to control the Bab el Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea, yet another oil chokepoint. The advance has posed a major challenge for the Saudis, who rely on that shipping route particularly since the Strait of Hormuz has been largely shuttered during the Iran war. The Houthis took control of Yemen in a bloody civil war in 2014 against a Saudi-backed coalition. A fragile truce between the Houthis and the Yemeni government backed by the U.N. was reached in 2022. Trump announced a ceasefire with the Houthis last year after weeks of punishing strikes against the militant group. Under the deal, the U.S. suspended military action and the Houthis stopped attacking U.S. ships. Trump recently has said his administration has had discussions with the Houthis but has not offered details. “The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved.”

articles.title: Former WHCA president on Trump’s press ban: ‘An attack on one outlet is an attack on everyone’
articles.summary: Former White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) president Weijia Jiang on Sunday said President Trump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters from covering the White House was an “attack” on all other news outlets. “This is not a tantrum by three media outlets who are upset because they can’t get into the White House…
articles.body:
Former White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) president Weijia Jiang on Sunday said President Trump’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters from covering the White House was an “attack” on all other news outlets.

“This is not a tantrum by three media outlets who are upset because they can’t get into the White House or the Oval Office,” Jiang, who is also CBS News’s senior White House correspondent, told Fox News’s Jacqui Heinrich on “ Fox News Sunday .” Heinrich is the WHCA’s current president.

“This is a serious concern for the public, because an attack on one outlet is an attack on everyone,” Jiang continued. “No matter where that outlet falls on the political spectrum. It is limiting the amount of information that reporters inside can gather, can excavate, to give back to the public.”

Jiang said that open access cannot be taken away just because the president does not like what is being reported. She also warned that it could set a precedent for future presidents on either side of the aisle.

“Look, every administration, every president hates the press,” she continued. “There should be tension. We wouldn’t be doing our jobs and, neither would they, if there wasn’t that friction.”

The former WHCA president said that covering the White House is an “absolute privilege” and that selecting who covers the president shrinks the viewpoints of who is in the building. It also costs voters the “currency” of information out of relationships reporters develop with White House staff and risks to shake the historical record, Jiang said.

“And all of that context matters in our reporting,” she added. “And that’s what we can’t do from outside the gate. And what you see sometimes might be at the edge of the frame, might not be captured if, for instance, the White House is running its own cameras.”

Heinrich noted that there is no major news outlet run by the federal government and asked what could happen if coverage is no longer independent from the government or the president.

“An America cannot have state TV,” Jiang replied. “That’s what makes America America … because you need independent actors to be able to be the observers. And if the government is only showing you what it wants, then you have to question: What are we missing?”

CNN, Politico and MS NOW announced in a joint statement on Monday that they will sue the administration “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.”

Trump, who accused the outlets of “constant” reporting of “FAKE NEWS,” issued the ban on Friday.

That same day, Trump said the White House “is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish.”

“It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” he added in a post on Truth Social.

Reporters from the three outlets were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated by the Secret Service. All three outlets condemned the ban, with several Fox News contributors slamming Trump’s decision.

articles.title: Appeals court seeks to revive GOP congressional map in Missouri
articles.summary: A federal appeals court on Monday introduced a new wrinkle into the convoluted fight over whether Republicans can use a new congressional map in November’s election, as the GOP tries to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic House districts.
articles.body: A federal appeals court on Monday introduced a new wrinkle into the convoluted fight over whether Republicans can use a new congressional map in November’s election, as the GOP tries to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic House districts. The St. Louis-based 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ordered that the new map drawn last year should be used this fall, even though the Supreme Court has already twice rejected Republicans on the issue in recent weeks and had apparently put the issue to bed. “This Court holds that Missouri’s current plan to use the 2022 map in the November 2026 general election violates the Constitution. Only use of the 2025 map complies with the Constitution and federal law,” the appeals court said in an unsigned ruling. The decision has no immediate effect and faces long odds to be implemented ahead of the election based on the Supreme Court’s previous action. The three-judge appeals court panel was comprised of Republican-appointed judges, including two picked by President Donald Trump. The appeals court put its ruling on hold for a week, giving the challengers time to seek Supreme Court intervention again. “Ballots have been printed, and Missourians have already voted. Thousands more will vote before this order seeks to take effect. Officials should stop wasting taxpayers’ money on pointless legal action and instead focus on administering our elections,” Richard von Glahn, the executive director of People Not Politicians, the group challenging the map, said in a statement. Monday’s decision upheld a decision by Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, who had that the new map must be used, notwithstanding the Missouri Supreme Court having previously reached the opposite conclusion. The U.S. Supreme Court put Clark’s ruling on hold on Sept. 10 in a decision that seemed to end the dispute, with the state set to use the previous map from 2022, which includes six seats held by Republicans and two held by Democrats. Missouri was one of several states where the Legislature drew a new map last year, seeking to draw out Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver and create a 7-1 GOP map. Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, had after a significant delay ordered election officials to use the 2022 map. That followed an unusual proceeding in which the Missouri Supreme Court held him in contempt for failing to comply with its ruling that said the 2025 map had to be put on hold under state law while a voter referendum takes place. The legal fight began when opponents of the new map gathered sufficient signatures to put the new map before voters in November as a ballot referendum. But Hoskins delayed a decision about whether to include the measure on the ballot, waiting until the last minute before rejecting the plan, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to voters’ approval.
